chant.name: Golden Chanterelle
chant.description: A golden yellow mushroom with a distinctive funnel shape and fruity aroma
chant.howTo: Look for them in deciduous forests, especially near oak and beech trees

guide.identify: Egg-yolk to golden yellow and up to 10 cm across, the cap a shallow funnel with a wavy, inrolled edge. Underneath are blunt, forking ridges that run down the stem; they cannot be lifted off one by one like gills. The stem is solid, the flesh white to pale yellow and firm, with a faint smell of apricots. Jack-o'-lanterns (Omphalotus) have thin, crowded true gills, grow in clusters from wood or buried roots and are orange right through; the false chanterelle (Hygrophoropsis aurantiaca) is deeper orange and soft, with thin, crowded gills.
guide.habitat: It lives with tree roots: under oak, beech, birch, chestnut, spruce and pine, mostly on acid soil in moss, often on banks and beside paths. Common across Europe, from the lowlands to the mountains. In North America the golden chanterelle is several close species, such as Cantharellus flavus in the East, C. californicus under live oaks in California and C. cascadensis in the Pacific Northwest.
guide.season: In central and northern Europe from late June to October, after warm, soaking rain; in southern Europe later and longer, into winter in Mediterranean oak woods. In the eastern US it fruits in summer after warm rain; in the West it follows the autumn rains and in California runs on into winter.
guide.picking: Cut or twist at the base, brush off soil on the spot and leave the small ones to grow. In Germany it is specially protected and may be picked only in small amounts for your own use; Swiss cantons, Italian regions, parts of France and Spain and US public lands set their own limits or permits, so check the local rules.
guide.kitchen: Once identified with certainty, brush chanterelles clean rather than washing them: they soak up water. Never eat them raw; cook them well, first in a dry pan until the water has gone, then in butter. Mild, fruity and slightly peppery, with a firm bite; good with eggs, cream, potatoes, pasta and chicken.
guide.keeps: A few days in the fridge in paper, not plastic. Dried chanterelles turn tough, so for longer keeping fry them in butter and freeze them.
guide.source: Identification and habitat: First Nature (UK) and MushroomExpert.com. North American species and look-alikes: University of Florida IFAS Extension. Protection: German Federal Species Protection Ordinance. Season: GBIF records.

mushroom.name: Porcini
mushroom.description: The king bolete: a stout brown-capped mushroom with a pale netted stem and white pores that never bruise blue
mushroom.howTo: Found in coniferous and deciduous forest, often near spruce and beech, from late summer into autumn

guide.identify: A stout bolete with a pale to chestnut-brown cap, smooth and greasy but never velvety, often with a thin whitish rim. The pores are white when young, then yellow and olive, and do not change colour when pressed. The pale stem has a fine white net near the top, and the white flesh does not change colour when cut. Pink pores and a dark brown net mean the bitter bolete (Tylopilus felleus); red or orange pores or bluing flesh mean another, possibly toxic bolete.
guide.habitat: With spruce, pine, beech, oak, sweet chestnut and birch on acid soil, from the lowlands to the tree line, across Europe. In North America it grows mainly in the Pacific states; the redder Rocky Mountain king is commoner in the southern Rockies.
guide.season: Mainly August to October, from June in the mountains and into November in the south; on the US Pacific coast with the autumn rains. A flush usually comes about two weeks after a soaking rain that follows a warm, dry spell.
guide.picking: Twist it out or cut it at the base; leave buttons and old or maggoty caps. Germany allows only small amounts for your own use, most Italian regions require a permit, and each US national forest sets its own rules.
guide.kitchen: Once it is identified with certainty, brush it clean, slice it lengthwise to check for maggots and fry it or use it in risotto, pasta and soups. Cook it through: not everyone tolerates it raw, and old or badly stored ones upset the stomach.
guide.keeps: Keep it cool in paper, not plastic, for a day or two. It dries very well in thin slices and freezes well.
guide.source: Identification and habitat: Regione Piemonte, First Nature and MushroomExpert. Season: GBIF records. Rules: BArtSchV (Germany) and US Forest Service. Cooking: Regione Piemonte and VIDAL.

morel.name: Morchella
morel.description: A distinctive mushroom with a honeycomb cap that appears in spring
morel.howTo: Look in disturbed areas, burned forests, and near dead trees in spring

guide.identify: The cap is a honeycomb of pits and ridges, yellowish, grey-brown or almost black, on a pale stem. Cut every one in half lengthways: a true morel is a single hollow from cap tip to stem base, with the cap joined to the stem at its lower edge. The deadly false morel (Gyromitra esculenta) has a brain-like, reddish-brown head and a chambered or cottony inside; cooking does not make it safe. Verpa bohemica has a cap attached only at the very top, like a thimble, and a stem stuffed with cottony pith.
guide.habitat: On the ground in open broadleaf and river woods, old orchards and gardens, often by ash, elm, poplar or apple, on lime-rich soil or bark mulch. In the eastern US, by dying elms, ash and old apple trees; in the western US, in conifer forest the spring after a fire.
guide.season: March to May: earlier in the lowlands of southern Europe, later in the north and in the mountains, into June. It follows soaking spring rain once the soil warms, and in the mountains of the western US the melting snow.
guide.picking: Cut the stem at ground level with a knife and carry morels in a basket or mesh bag. In Germany all morels are protected: small amounts for your own use only. Elsewhere many regions and US national forests set limits or ask for a permit: check local rules.
guide.kitchen: Once identified with certainty, morels must be cooked thoroughly: raw or undercooked, dried ones included, they are toxic. France's food-safety agency ANSES advises 20 to 30 minutes in the pan for wild mushrooms. Large meals have caused dizziness and trembling even when cooked, so keep portions modest; they suit butter, cream, asparagus and chicken.
guide.keeps: Two days in the fridge, in a paper bag. They dry very well; soak dried morels, strain the water into the sauce and cook them as long as fresh ones.
guide.source: Identification and habitat: Missouri Department of Conservation and First Nature. Toxicity and cooking: ANSES and Lagrange and Vernoux (Toxins, 2020). Rules: German Federal Species Protection Ordinance and US Forest Service. Season: GBIF records.

blackberry.name: Blackberry
blackberry.description: Sweet, dark purple berries that grow on thorny bushes
blackberry.howTo: Found in hedgerows, woodland edges, and disturbed areas in late summer

guide.identify: A bramble with long, arching stems armed with hooked prickles; the leaves have three or five toothed leaflets spread like a hand, dark green above and paler beneath. White or pink five-petalled flowers give berries made of many small round drupelets, green then red then glossy black. A ripe blackberry comes off with its white core inside; a raspberry leaves its core on the plant and is hollow. Rubus fruticosus is a group of hundreds of closely related brambles, all used the same way.
guide.habitat: Hedgerows, woodland edges and clearings, scrub, wasteland and railway banks, on almost any soil, across Europe except the far north. In the US, native blackberries grow in old fields and woodland edges, and the introduced Himalayan blackberry forms dense thickets in the Pacific Northwest and California.
guide.season: Ripens from July in the south of Europe and the US and from late July or August further north, and goes on until the first frosts in September and October; flowers, green fruit and ripe fruit often hang on the same bush.
guide.picking: Pick only fully black berries that come away with a gentle pull, leave the red ones and some for wildlife, and avoid busy roadsides and edges sprayed with weedkiller. In central Europe, Bavaria's health authority (LGL) says eating wild berries has not been shown to be a risk factor for fox tapeworm, but advises washing them well; only heating above 60 °C kills its eggs, and home freezing does not.
guide.kitchen: Once identified with certainty, the berries are eaten raw or cooked: in crumbles and pies with apple, in jam, jelly, syrup and vinegar. Rinse them just before use and check for insects. The flavour ranges from sweet to sharp from bush to bush.
guide.keeps: Unwashed and spread in a shallow box, they keep a day or two in the fridge. To freeze, spread them on a tray and bag them once hard; frozen berries suit cooking.
guide.source: Identification, habitat and uses: Woodland Trust. Fox tapeworm: Bavarian State Office for Health and Food Safety (LGL).

elderberry.name: Elderberry
elderberry.description: Small dark purple berries that grow in clusters on elder trees
elderberry.howTo: Look for elder trees in hedgerows and woodland edges in autumn

guide.identify: A shrub or small tree with grey-brown, corky, furrowed bark and soft white pith inside the twigs. The leaves are opposite, with five to seven toothed leaflets (up to eleven in American elderberry); flat heads of creamy, scented flowers in early summer become broad clusters of small purple-black berries on reddish stalks, which droop under their weight when ripe. Dwarf elder (Sambucus ebulus) is a soft herb that dies back each winter, with berry clusters standing upright above the leaves; red elder (Sambucus racemosa) has red berries in upright, dome-shaped clusters. Pokeweed (Phytolacca americana) is a tall herb with smooth purple-red stems and berries strung along long spikes, not in flat clusters.
guide.habitat: Hedgerows, woodland edges, scrub, riverbanks, wasteland and the edges of villages, on rich, moist soil, across Europe except the far north. In the eastern US the native American elderberry grows along streams, wet ditches and field edges; in the west, blue elderberry, whose ripe berries carry a dusty blue bloom, grows on open slopes and in valleys.
guide.season: Berries ripen in early autumn: from late August in warm lowlands, through September and into October further north and in the mountains. The creamy flower heads come earlier, from late May.
guide.picking: Cut whole clusters with scissors when every berry is purple-black, and leave clusters with green or red berries. Avoid busy roadsides and leave plenty on each bush for birds.
guide.kitchen: Elderberries must be cooked: raw or unripe berries, stems, leaves and seeds contain compounds that release cyanide during digestion and can cause nausea, vomiting and stomach cramps; thorough cooking breaks them down. Once identified with certainty, strip the berries from the stalks with a fork, discard green berries and every bit of stem, and simmer them into syrup, jelly, juice, soup or pie filling. The taste is dark, earthy and tart and goes well with apple, pear, cinnamon and lemon; never use red elderberries for food.
guide.keeps: Fresh clusters keep a day or two in the fridge. Frozen whole, the berries shake off the stalks easily; frozen or dried berries must still be cooked before eating.
guide.source: Identification and habitat: Woodland Trust. Toxicity, cooking and keeping: Oregon State University Extension.

nettle.name: Nettle
nettle.description: A nutritious green plant with stinging hairs that must be cooked
nettle.howTo: Found in disturbed areas, hedgerows, and woodland edges in spring and summer

guide.identify: An upright plant with square stems and leaves in opposite pairs: heart-shaped to oval, coarsely toothed and pointed. Stems and leaves are covered in stinging hairs, and from early summer thin tassels of tiny greenish flowers hang where the leaves join the stem. Dead-nettles look similar but do not sting and have showy white, yellow or purple lipped flowers.
guide.habitat: Grows in dense patches on rich, moist soil: woodland edges, riverbanks, ditches, hedgerows and the ground around farms and old buildings. Common throughout Europe, in the south mostly in damp, shaded places, and across most of the US, especially along streams and in moist open woods.
guide.season: Young shoots appear from February in mild areas and in March further north; pick them until the plant flowers, from about June. Cut or mown patches send up fresh shoots for a second picking in late summer and autumn.
guide.picking: Wear gloves, snip the top few pairs of leaves with scissors and leave the roots. Avoid roadsides, sprayed field edges and dog-walking paths; nettle patches also feed the caterpillars of many butterflies.
guide.kitchen: Always cook or blanch nettles before eating them: heat removes the sting, and so does thorough drying. Drop the washed tops into boiling salted water for a few minutes, then use them like spinach in soups, risotto, omelettes and pesto; they taste like spinach with an earthy edge.
guide.keeps: Blanched, squeezed and frozen in portions they keep for months; leaves dried in a shady, airy place make tea.
guide.source: Identification, habitat and cooking: NC State Extension and Woodland Trust. Season: Woodland Trust and GBIF records.

dandelion.name: Dandelion
dandelion.description: A common weed with bright yellow flowers and edible leaves
dandelion.howTo: Found in meadows, grasslands, and disturbed areas during growing season

guide.identify: Dandelion grows as a ground-level rosette of hairless leaves, deeply and raggedly lobed, with teeth that point back towards the centre. Leaves and stalks bleed white milky sap when broken; each flower stalk is leafless, unbranched and hollow and carries one head of yellow, strap-shaped florets, followed by a round white seed clock. Cat's-ear has branched, solid stalks and hairy leaves, hawkbits have forked hairs on the leaves and sow-thistles carry several flowers on leafy stems: pick only plants that match every point.
guide.habitat: Lawns, meadows, pastures, verges and waste ground, in sun, from the lowlands into the mountains. It grows almost everywhere in Europe and, brought from Europe, throughout the US.
guide.season: A big flush of flowers comes in early spring, mainly in April and May and earlier in the mild south, then flowers appear on and off until autumn. The leaves are least bitter in early spring, before the first buds appear.
guide.picking: Cut young leaves at the base and pick flowers on a sunny day when they are fully open, leaving plenty for early bees. Avoid lawns treated with weedkiller, roadsides and places where dogs are walked, and dig roots only where you have the landowner's permission, such as your own garden.
guide.kitchen: Once identified with certainty, young leaves are eaten raw in salads, pleasantly bitter, as in the French salad with bacon; older leaves are boiled for about 10 minutes to take off some bitterness, then fried with garlic and oil. Use the flowers cooked, in fritters or simmered with sugar and lemon into a thick syrup, and roast cleaned roots for a coffee substitute; eaten in quantity, the roots are a laxative. The milky sap can irritate skin, and people allergic to the daisy family can react, so try a small amount first.
guide.keeps: Leaves keep a few days in a bag in the fridge. Use flowers straight after picking, as they close quickly; roasted roots keep in an airtight jar.
guide.source: Identification: BSBI and NC State Extension. Picking and cooking: University of Wisconsin-Madison Extension and Colorado State University Extension. Safety: US National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health.

hazelnut.name: Hazelnut
hazelnut.description: Sweet, round nuts that grow on hazel trees
hazelnut.howTo: Look for hazel trees in hedgerows and woodland edges in autumn

guide.identify: A shrub or small tree with many stems and round, doubly toothed leaves, pointed at the tip and soft and downy underneath; yellow catkins hang from bare twigs in late winter. The nuts grow in bunches of one to four, each in a frilly green leafy husk covering about three quarters of it, and turn brown as they ripen. North America's wild hazels are close relatives; the beaked hazelnut's husk forms a long bristly tube.
guide.habitat: Woodland understorey, hedgerows and scrub across Europe, in the south mostly in hills and mountains; it fruits best in sun at woodland edges. In the US the European hazel grows mainly in Oregon orchards; the wild species grow in thickets, clearings and woodland edges.
guide.season: Late August to October: the nuts are ready when the husk browns and they fall or come loose with a light shake. Squirrels, jays and dormice often get there first.
guide.picking: Gather fallen nuts or shake the branches lightly, and leave plenty for wildlife. Skip nuts with a small round hole (a weevil larva has eaten the kernel) and light ones, and avoid busy roadsides and sprayed field edges.
guide.kitchen: Once you are sure of the plant, eat them raw or roast them until the skins crack, then rub the skins off in a rough cloth. Use them in cakes, pralines, pesto and salads. Hazelnuts are a common cause of nut allergy.
guide.keeps: Dry them in the shell in an airy place until the kernel turns cream right through, then store them cool and dry; dried nuts keep up to a year in the fridge.
guide.source: Identification and habitat: Woodland Trust and Minnesota Department of Natural Resources. Drying and storage: Oregon State University Extension.

garlic.name: Wild Garlic
garlic.description: A pungent herb with broad leaves and white flowers
garlic.howTo: Found in deciduous woodlands in spring, often forming large patches

guide.identify: Each leaf grows on its own thin stalk straight from the ground: a soft, bright green, pointed oval blade with parallel veins, matt underneath; from April a leafless stalk carries a rounded cluster of white, star-shaped flowers. Crush a leaf: wild garlic smells strongly of garlic and its deadly look-alikes do not, but the smell stays on your fingers, so after the first few leaves the test proves nothing; check every leaf by its stalk and outline too. Lily of the valley has two or three leaves wrapped around one another at the base; autumn crocus has tough, stalkless leaves in a tuft; lords-and-ladies has arrow-shaped leaves with net veins; white false hellebore has pleated leaves along an upright stem; Solomon's seal has leaves alternating along an arching stem.
guide.habitat: Forms carpets in damp, shady deciduous woods, especially beech and floodplain woods on rich soil, and along shaded streams. Common in central and northern Europe, including Britain; in southern Europe mostly in mountain woods.
guide.season: Leaves come up from February in mild places and in March and April elsewhere, and are best before the flowers open. It flowers from April to June, later in the mountains; by early summer the leaves are gone.
guide.picking: Pick leaf by leaf, never by the handful, so that no look-alike growing in the same patch ends up in your basket, and leave the bulbs. Britain bans digging up wild plants without the landowner's permission, Germany allows only a small amount for your own use and many nature reserves ban picking: check local rules.
guide.kitchen: Once identified with certainty, use the leaves raw or add them at the end of cooking: in pesto, soups, risotto, butter and with eggs; the flowers go on salads. Wash each leaf under running water: in central Europe authorities advise this because of fox tapeworm, whose eggs survive freezing but not cooking.
guide.keeps: Leaves keep two or three days in the fridge in a damp cloth. Chopped leaves and pesto freeze well; keep anything in oil in the fridge and use it within a few days.
guide.source: Identification and look-alikes: Austrian Agency for Health and Food Safety (AGES), German Federal Institute for Risk Assessment (BfR) and Woodland Trust. Season: Woodland Trust and GBIF records.

chickenOfTheWoods.name: Chicken of the Woods
chickenOfTheWoods.description: A bright orange-yellow bracket fungus that grows on trees
chickenOfTheWoods.howTo: Look for it growing on dead or dying trees, especially oaks

guide.identify: Overlapping, fan-shaped brackets 10 to 40 cm wide with no stem: soft, moist and bright yellow to orange when young, fading to cream and turning chalky with age. The underside is sulphur-yellow with tiny pores, not gills; the flesh is white to pale yellow and does not change colour when cut. An orange cluster on wood with gills underneath is the poisonous jack-o'-lantern (Omphalotus). In the western US the closely related Laetiporus gilbertsonii and Laetiporus conifericola look much the same.
guide.habitat: A wood-decay fungus on living and dead broadleaf trees, most often oak, also sweet chestnut, cherry, willow and beech, and now and then yew. It is common in lowland Europe and the eastern US, in woods, parks and streets; in the western US its relatives grow on oaks, eucalyptus and conifers.
guide.season: Late spring to autumn, mostly in summer, a few days after warm rain; in the western US mainly in autumn. The same tree often fruits for several years.
guide.picking: Cut the soft edges of young brackets with a knife and leave the tough base and old, chalky brackets. Never pick it from yew, which is highly poisonous, or from trees along busy roads; where mushroom picking needs a permit or has daily limits, check local rules.
guide.kitchen: Once identified with certainty, cook it thoroughly: raw or undercooked it upsets the stomach, and even well cooked it disagrees with some people (nausea, dizziness, vomiting), so try a small amount first. Sliced and fried or braised, the firm flesh is often compared to chicken and goes with lemon, garlic and herbs.
guide.keeps: A few days in the fridge in a paper bag. It freezes well, raw or cooked.
guide.source: Identification and hosts: Woodland Trust, First Nature and MushroomExpert.com. Western species: Bay Area Mycological Society. Reactions: University of Florida IFAS Extension.

oysterMushroom.name: Oyster Mushroom
oysterMushroom.description: A white-grey mushroom with fan-shaped cap that grows in clusters on dead wood
oysterMushroom.howTo: Look for them growing on dead trees, especially beech and oak, in autumn and winter

guide.identify: A shell- or fan-shaped cap 5 to 18 cm across, blue-grey, grey-brown or cream, in overlapping tiers on wood. White to cream gills run down into a short, off-centre stem or none; the flesh is white and firm, the smell mild and the spore print white to pale lilac. The poisonous jack-o'-lantern (Omphalotus) is bright orange, gills included, and grows in tufts at the foot of trees; sulphur tuft (Hypholoma fasciculare) has sulphur-yellow caps on central stems, greenish-yellow gills turning purple-brown and a bitter taste. Angel wings (Pleurocybella porrigens), linked to deaths in Japan, are pure white, thin and translucent and grow only on rotting conifer wood.
guide.habitat: On dead or dying broadleaf trees, mainly beech, also poplar, willow, oak and ash: standing trunks, stumps and fallen logs, rarely conifers. Common across Europe and North America.
guide.season: Late autumn into winter, set off by a cold spell or the first frosts after rain; into January or February in southern Europe and from October to early April in the eastern US.
guide.picking: Cut the cluster at the base with a knife, take firm young caps and leave old or beetle-riddled ones. Where mushroom picking needs a permit or has daily limits, check local rules.
guide.kitchen: Once identified with certainty, cook it well; do not eat it raw. Trim the tough base, tear the caps into strips and fry them hot until the edges crisp; the mild, slightly sweet taste goes with garlic, butter, soy sauce and eggs.
guide.keeps: It spoils fast: keep it in a paper bag in the fridge for a few days, or freeze it after cooking.
guide.source: Identification and season: First Nature and MushroomExpert.com. Angel wings: Beaty Biodiversity Museum, University of British Columbia.

shiitake.name: Shiitake
shiitake.description: A mushroom with brown cap and white gills, highly prized in Asian cuisine
shiitake.howTo: Found growing on dead hardwood trees, especially oak and beech, in spring and autumn

guide.identify: A brown to dark reddish-brown cap that flattens with age, often with whitish flecks near the edge and cracks in dry weather. The gills are white to cream and bruise brown; the stem is tough, fibrous and often off-centre; the spore print is white. The deadly funeral bell (Galerina marginata) also grows on logs: it is smaller and honey-brown, with a ring on the stem and a rusty-brown spore print.
guide.habitat: Native to East Asia, on dead broadleaf wood such as oak and Castanopsis. In Europe and North America it is grown on oak logs or sawdust blocks and has been found outside cultivation only a few times (for example in the Netherlands), so a brown mushroom on a fallen log in the woods is almost certainly something else.
guide.season: Logs kept outdoors fruit in spring and autumn, a few days after soaking rain in mild weather; growers also force a flush by soaking a log in cold water.
guide.picking: Pick caps while the edge is still curled under: twist them off or cut the stem at the log. Pick only from logs you grow or have permission to pick from.
guide.kitchen: Once identified with certainty, cook it thoroughly: raw or lightly cooked shiitake can cause shiitake dermatitis, an itchy rash of whip-like streaks about a day later. The stems are too tough to eat but flavour stock; fry or simmer the caps, which have a deep, savoury taste, with soy sauce, ginger and garlic.
guide.keeps: A few days in the fridge in a paper bag. It dries very well: soak dried caps before use and keep the water as stock.
guide.source: Origin and distribution: Naturalis Biodiversity Center. Log growing: Cornell Cooperative Extension. Shiitake dermatitis: DermNet.

raspberry.name: Wild Raspberry
raspberry.description: Sweet red berries that grow on thorny canes with distinctive compound leaves
raspberry.howTo: Look for raspberry canes in hedgerows, woodland edges, and disturbed areas in summer

guide.identify: Upright canes, often head-high, covered in small, fine prickles rather than the hooked thorns of a blackberry. The leaves have three to seven toothed leaflets set along a stalk, green above and white-felted beneath. Small white flowers hang downwards; the red berry comes away from the plant leaving its white core behind, so a picked raspberry is a hollow cap.
guide.habitat: Woodland clearings and edges, felled and burnt ground, scrub, heathland, rocky slopes and hedgerows, from the lowlands into the mountains across Europe; it moves into new clearings and fades as the trees grow back. In the US, American red raspberry grows across the north and in the western mountains, and the black raspberry, with purple-black hollow berries, in the east.
guide.season: Ripens in summer: from June in southern Europe and the lowlands, in July and August in the north and in the mountains, sometimes into September up high.
guide.picking: Pick berries that are fully red and slip off the core without pulling, into a shallow container, as they crush easily. In central Europe, Bavaria's health authority (LGL) says eating wild berries has not been shown to be a risk factor for fox tapeworm, but advises washing them well; only heating above 60 °C kills its eggs, and home freezing does not.
guide.kitchen: Once identified with certainty, eat them raw or use them for jam, syrup, cakes and desserts; wild raspberries are smaller and more aromatic than garden ones. Rinse them briefly just before use and check for the small white larvae of the raspberry beetle.
guide.keeps: Very perishable: eat them the same day or keep them a day or two in the fridge, unwashed. Freeze them spread on a tray, then bag them; frozen berries suit sauces and baking.
guide.source: Identification and habitat: Woodland Trust. Fox tapeworm: Bavarian State Office for Health and Food Safety (LGL).

blueberry.name: Wild Blueberry
blueberry.description: Small sweet blue berries that grow on low shrubs in acidic soil
blueberry.howTo: Found in heaths, moors, and acidic forests in summer and early autumn

guide.identify: Bilberry, also called whortleberry, is a low deciduous shrub, usually below knee height, with green, angled stems and small oval leaves with finely toothed edges. Pinkish, lantern-shaped flowers hang singly in spring; each gives one blue-black berry with a pale bloom and a small crown-shaped ring at the tip, and the flesh is purple-red right through (cultivated blueberries have pale flesh). Its poisonous look-alikes are soft herbs, not woody dwarf shrubs: deadly nightshade (Atropa bella-donna) is tall, with shiny black berries sitting in a green star of five sepals; herb Paris (Paris quadrifolia) carries one berry on top of a stem with a whorl of four leaves; Solomon's seal (Polygonatum) hangs blue-black berries beneath an arching, unbranched stem.
guide.habitat: Acid, nutrient-poor soil: conifer, birch and oak woods, heaths and moorland, from the lowlands to above the treeline; common across northern and central Europe and in the mountains of the south, and absent on lime. In North America it grows wild in the western mountains; in the east, the wild blueberries picked are lowbush and highbush blueberries (Vaccinium angustifolium, Vaccinium corymbosum), close relatives with pale flesh.
guide.season: Ripens from July in the lowlands; in the mountains and the north the season runs through August into September. A late frost at flowering can cut the crop.
guide.picking: Pick by hand: berry combs strip leaves and damage the plants, and some places ban them or set daily limits, such as the Vosges in France and Tuscany in Italy: check local rules. In central Europe, Bavaria's health authority (LGL) says eating wild berries has not been shown to be a risk factor for fox tapeworm, but advises washing them well; only heating above 60 °C kills its eggs, and home freezing does not.
guide.kitchen: Once identified with certainty, eat them raw or in tarts, pancakes, jam and compote; they are sweet and sharp and stain fingers, teeth and clothes. Rinse them briefly just before use and pick out leaves and green berries.
guide.keeps: They keep a few days in the fridge, unwashed and spread out. Freeze them on a tray, then bag them; they also dry well.
guide.source: Identification and habitat: Woodland Trust; look-alikes: Yle (Finnish public broadcaster). Picking rules: Vosges prefecture and Region of Tuscany. Fox tapeworm: Bavarian State Office for Health and Food Safety (LGL).

strawberry.name: Wild Strawberry
strawberry.description: Small red berries with intense flavor, with white flowers and trifoliate leaves
strawberry.howTo: Look for them in meadows, woodland edges, and grassy areas in spring and summer

guide.identify: A low plant with long-stalked leaves of three toothed leaflets, bright green and slightly glossy, spreading by runners that root along the ground; the end tooth of each leaflet is as long as its neighbours or longer. The flowers are white with five rounded petals and a yellow centre; the fruit is a small red cone with tiny seeds on the surface, hanging from a thin stalk. Barren strawberry (Potentilla sterilis) flowers earlier and has gaps between its notched petals, an end tooth shorter than its neighbours and no fleshy fruit; mock strawberry (Potentilla indica) has yellow flowers and round, spongy, tasteless berries.
guide.habitat: Woodland edges, clearings, sunny banks, path sides, hedgerow bases and old grassland, often on dry, stony or lime-rich soil, from the lowlands into the mountains across Europe. In the US it grows in open woods and clearings in the north and in the western mountains; the larger Virginia strawberry (Fragaria virginiana) is the usual wild strawberry of fields and meadows.
guide.season: Flowers from April; berries ripen from late May in southern Europe and from June elsewhere, and plants keep fruiting through the summer, into August in the mountains and the north.
guide.picking: Pick only fully red berries by pinching the stalk and never pull up the plants; in England, where wild strawberry is listed as near threatened, pick sparingly. In central Europe, Bavaria's health authority (LGL) says eating wild berries has not been shown to be a risk factor for fox tapeworm, but advises washing them well; only heating above 60 °C kills its eggs, and home freezing does not.
guide.kitchen: Once identified with certainty, eat them raw and soon, rinsed briefly just before eating. The flavour is more intense than that of garden strawberries but varies from plant to plant; a handful is enough to scent cream, yoghurt or a tart.
guide.keeps: They spoil quickly in a warm basket: keep them cool and eat them the same day. They can be frozen, but thaw soft.
guide.source: Identification and habitat: Woodland Trust and Botanical Society of Britain and Ireland (BSBI). Fox tapeworm: Bavarian State Office for Health and Food Safety (LGL).

wildMint.name: Wild mints
wildMint.description: Any wild mint: water mint, horse mint, apple mint, corn mint and pennyroyal. Square stems, opposite leaves and a mint scent when crushed
wildMint.howTo: Found in damp ground, ditches and along streams. Pennyroyal is fine as a light tea (poleo menta) but toxic as an oil or in quantity: avoid it in pregnancy

guide.identify: All mints have square stems, leaves in opposite pairs and a clear mint smell when a leaf is crushed; small lilac, pink or white flowers grow in whorls or in heads and spikes at the shoot tips. Water mint has hairy, oval leaves and a rounded flower head; horse mint long, grey-hairy leaves; apple mint round, wrinkled, soft leaves; corn mint flowers only in whorls along the stem; pennyroyal is small and creeping, with tiny leaves and a sharp smell. Unscented square-stemmed plants such as gipsywort grow among them, and the smell stays on your fingers: smell each stem on its own and leave any that does not smell of mint.
guide.habitat: Most wild mints like wet ground: stream and pond edges, ditches, marshes and wet meadows; corn mint also grows in damp fields and pennyroyal in grassland that floods in winter, mostly in southern and western Europe. In the US the native American wild mint grows in wet places across most of the country, and spearmint, peppermint and pennyroyal have escaped from gardens.
guide.season: Shoots appear in spring and are most tender before flowering; most flower from midsummer into autumn, and growth starts earlier in southern Europe.
guide.picking: Pinch off the top few pairs of leaves above a leaf joint and leave the roots. Pick stem by stem, not by the handful: deadly hemlock water-dropwort and water hemlock grow in the same wet places; avoid water below farms or sewage outlets.
guide.kitchen: Once identified with certainty, the leaves make tea and go into salads, yoghurt sauces and dishes with peas, potatoes and lamb. Mint from streams, ditches or grazed wet pasture can carry liver fluke, like wild watercress: use it only in hot tea or cooked. Pennyroyal contains pulegone, which harms the liver: a light tea is traditional in Spain and Portugal, but never use the oil, never drink it strong or often, and never give it to babies, children or anyone pregnant, breastfeeding or with liver disease.
guide.keeps: Bunches hung in a dark, airy place dry well for tea; chopped leaves freeze in ice cubes.
guide.source: Identification and habitat: Botanical Society of Britain and Ireland, The Wildlife Trusts and Native Plant Trust (Go Botany). Pennyroyal: European Medicines Agency and National Capital Poison Center. Liver fluke: Pan American Health Organization. Season: GBIF records.

chickweed.name: Chickweed
chickweed.description: A low-growing plant with small white flowers and oval leaves, very nutritious
chickweed.howTo: Common in gardens, disturbed areas, and meadows during growing season

guide.identify: A low, sprawling plant with weak, round, juicy stems and small, pointed oval leaves in opposite pairs, the lower ones on short stalks. A single line of fine hairs runs down the stem, switching sides at each leaf pair. The white, star-shaped flowers have five petals split so deeply that they look like ten. Two toxic look-alikes: scarlet pimpernel has square, hairless stems, stalkless leaves with black dots underneath and orange-red or blue flowers; spurges ooze white, milky sap from a broken stem, which chickweed never does.
guide.habitat: Gardens, vegetable beds, field edges, farmyards and other disturbed, rich, moist soil, often in light shade. One of the commonest plants in Europe and found across the US.
guide.season: Grows best in cool, damp weather: spring and autumn in the north, autumn to spring in mild areas such as southern Europe and the southern US. Summer heat and drought make it die back until the autumn rains.
guide.picking: Snip or pinch off the leafy top few centimetres; the plant regrows. Pick only where no weedkiller has been sprayed, away from roads and from spots where dogs and cats go.
guide.kitchen: Once identified with certainty, the leaves, stems and flowers are eaten raw or briefly cooked; they taste mild and fresh, a little like young peas. Add them to salads, sandwiches and pesto, or stir them into soups at the end, and wash them well.
guide.keeps: Chickweed wilts quickly: keep it in a bag in the fridge and eat it within a day or two.
guide.source: Identification: UC Statewide IPM Program and Woodland Trust. Scarlet pimpernel: Ontario Ministry of Agriculture. Season: Woodland Trust and GBIF records.

plantain.name: Common Plantain
plantain.description: A low-growing plant with broad oval leaves and tall flower spikes
plantain.howTo: Found in lawns, meadows, and disturbed areas during growing season

guide.identify: Common plantain grows as a flat rosette of broad, oval leaves on short, wide stalks; each leaf has three to seven strong veins running side by side from base to tip, and if you snap a leaf stalk they pull out as tough strings. From early summer, leafless stalks carry long, narrow rat-tail spikes of tiny greenish flowers, later full of small brown seeds. The first-year rosette of foxglove, which is deadly, has soft, hairy, wrinkled leaves with a net of veins and no strings; foxglove leaves have been sold by mistake as plantain.
guide.habitat: Lawns, paths, farm tracks, field edges, meadows and gardens: wherever the ground is trampled and compacted. Native to Europe and Asia, it is common all over Europe and across the whole of the US, where it came with European settlers.
guide.season: New leaves appear from early spring to autumn, most tender in spring and after mowing. Flower spikes rise from early summer and the seeds ripen into autumn.
guide.picking: Pick young leaves from the centre of the rosette, a few from each plant, and leave the root in the ground. Avoid roadsides, paths used by dogs and lawns or verges that may have been sprayed with weedkiller.
guide.kitchen: Once identified with certainty, young leaves can go raw into salads; older leaves are tough and stringy, so blanch them or cook them like spinach and pull out the strings. The taste is mild, grassy and slightly bitter. NC State Extension notes that very large amounts can lower blood pressure: eat it as one green among others.
guide.keeps: The leaves wilt fast: keep them in a bag in the fridge for a day or two, or dry them in the shade for tea.
guide.source: Identification, habitat and season: NC State Extension, Michigan State University Extension and UC IPM. Foxglove mix-up: US FDA (1997). Kitchen: NC State Extension.

walnut.name: Walnut
walnut.description: Large round nuts with hard shells and rich, oily flavor
walnut.howTo: Look for walnut trees in parks, gardens, and woodland edges in autumn

guide.identify: A large tree with smooth olive-brown bark that turns grey and fissured with age, and leaves of five to nine smooth-edged oval leaflets that smell of polish when crushed. The nut sits in a thick, smooth green husk that darkens and splits when ripe. The black walnut of the eastern US has more, narrower, toothed leaflets and a round husk that does not split, around a very hard, ridged shell.
guide.habitat: Native from south-east Europe to south-west China, it has been planted across Europe and gone wild in hedgerows, field edges, riverbanks and young woods, mostly at low altitude on deep, fertile soil. In the US, orchards are mainly in California; in the eastern woods the wild species is the black walnut.
guide.season: September and October, when the husks crack and the nuts drop. Green walnuts for pickling or liqueur are picked in late June or early July, while a skewer still goes straight through.
guide.picking: Gather fallen nuts every day or two, before mould and insects spoil them, and wear gloves: the husk stains skin brown for days. Remove the husks soon; most walnut trees belong to someone, so ask first.
guide.kitchen: Once you are sure of the tree, eat fresh walnuts with the bitter skin peeled off, or dry them for bread, cakes, salads and sauces. Throw away mouldy, shrivelled or rancid kernels. Walnuts are a common cause of nut allergy.
guide.keeps: Dry them in the shell in an airy, shady place until the divider between the halves snaps; dried nuts keep up to a year in the fridge.
guide.source: Identification and range: Woodland Trust. Harvest and storage: Oregon State University and Kansas State University extension.

chestnut.name: Chestnut
chestnut.description: Large sweet nuts encased in spiny green husks that split open when ripe
chestnut.howTo: Found in chestnut groves and mixed forests in autumn, often near paths

guide.identify: Long, narrow, glossy leaves 16 to 28 cm long with sharp saw teeth and many straight, parallel veins. The husk is covered all over with long, fine, needle-sharp spines and usually holds two or three nuts, flattened on one or both sides and ending in a small point with a tuft. The toxic horse chestnut (Aesculus hippocastanum) of parks and streets has hand-shaped leaves of five to seven leaflets, a thick green husk with a few short spikes and one or two round, glossy conkers with no point. In North America the buckeyes (other Aesculus) are toxic too: a tree with hand-shaped leaves is never a sweet chestnut.
guide.habitat: Native to southern Europe, western Asia and North Africa and long planted for its nuts, it grows on acid, well-drained soil and avoids limestone; large chestnut woods cover hills from northern Portugal and Galicia to the Cévennes, Corsica and the Apennines. In the US most chestnuts are planted, as blight nearly wiped out the native species.
guide.season: The nuts fall from late September to early November, mostly in October, earlier in the lowlands than in the mountains.
guide.picking: Every few days, gather nuts that have fallen on their own; wear thick gloves or roll the husks open under your boot, and leave nuts with small holes from weevil or moth larvae. Many chestnut woods are private and the nuts on the ground belong to the owner: check local rules.
guide.kitchen: Once you are sure they are sweet chestnuts, cook them: raw they are astringent and hard to digest. Discard any that float in water, cut a slit in the shell so they do not burst, then roast them or simmer them for about 30 minutes and peel off the shell and bitter inner skin while warm. Sweet and floury, they go into soups, stuffings and purées.
guide.keeps: Fresh chestnuts mould within about two weeks at room temperature; in the fridge they keep about two months, or freeze or dry them.
guide.source: Identification: Woodland Trust, ANSES and Oregon State University Extension. Harvest, cooking and storage: Oregon State University Extension.

elderflower.name: Elderflower
elderflower.description: Creamy white flowers that grow in large flat clusters on elder trees
elderflower.howTo: Look for elder trees in hedgerows and woodland edges in late spring and early summer

guide.identify: Elder is a woody shrub or small tree with corky, furrowed, grey-brown bark and opposite leaves of 5 to 7 toothed leaflets that smell unpleasant when crushed. In late spring it carries flat, branching heads of tiny creamy white flowers with pale yellow anthers and a sweet, musky scent. Danewort (dwarf elder) is a soft herb that dies back each winter, with upright heads and purple anthers, and red elder flowers earlier in egg- or dome-shaped clusters; both are toxic. Hemlock, water hemlock and giant hogweed, whose sap burns skin in sunlight, are soft green herbs, not woody shrubs: hemlock has a smooth, hollow, purple-blotched stem and a mousy smell, and in all three the flower stalks spread from one point like umbrella spokes.
guide.habitat: Hedgerows, woodland edges, scrub, riverbanks and waste ground, often near houses on rich soil; common across Europe from the lowlands into the hills. In the US the native American elder in the East and blue elder in the West grow in similar places.
guide.season: Elder flowers from late May into June in northern and central Europe, earlier in the warm south. In the eastern US American elder flowers later and over a longer spell, mostly in June and July.
guide.picking: Pick on a dry, sunny morning, choosing heads that are fully open, creamy and sweet-smelling, and pass over browning ones. Cut or snap them at the base, take only a few from each bush so it can still bear berries, and shake out insects gently.
guide.kitchen: Once identified with certainty, only the flowers are used: strip them from the stalks, since stalks, leaves, bark, roots and unripe berries are poisonous. Steep them in hot sugar syrup with lemon for cordial, dip whole heads in batter and fry them as fritters without eating the thick stalk, or dry them for tea; the taste is sweet and floral, good with gooseberries and strawberries. The berries that follow in autumn must be cooked.
guide.keeps: The flowers fade fast, so use them the day you pick them. Heads dried in the shade keep for tea in an airtight jar; cordial keeps a few weeks in the fridge or can be frozen.
guide.source: Identification and habitat: Woodland Trust and BSBI. Look-alikes: University of Minnesota Extension. Picking and cooking: Penn State Extension and UMass Extension.

daisy.name: Common Daisy
daisy.description: Small white flowers with yellow centers that grow close to the ground
daisy.howTo: Common in lawns, meadows, and grassy areas during spring and summer

guide.identify: The common daisy is a low plant with a flat rosette of spoon-shaped, slightly hairy leaves pressed to the ground. Each leafless, hairy stalk carries one flower head about 2 cm across: white rays, often tipped with pink, around a yellow centre; the heads close at night and in dull weather. Bigger daisy-like flowers on leafy stems, such as oxeye daisy, and the mayweeds and chamomiles with feathery leaves are different plants.
guide.habitat: Lawns, short turf, grazed pastures, verges and paths, in sun on moist soil; it grows almost everywhere in Europe. In the US it came from Europe and now grows in lawns and damp, disturbed ground, most of all where summers are cool.
guide.season: It flowers almost all year where winters are mild, with the main flush from spring into early summer. In cold regions and much of the US it flowers from spring to early summer, with scattered flowers until frost.
guide.picking: Pinch off flower heads and a few young leaves, taking from many plants and leaving the rosettes in place. Avoid lawns treated with weedkiller or fertiliser, places where dogs are walked and roadsides.
guide.kitchen: Once identified with certainty, the flowers and young leaves are eaten raw in small amounts, in salads and sandwiches or as a garnish; they taste mild to slightly bitter, and older leaves are tough. Rinse them gently in cool water. Try only a little at first, since people allergic to the daisy family can react and large amounts can upset the stomach, and avoid it in pregnancy and while breastfeeding.
guide.keeps: Pick just before use, as the flowers wilt quickly; until then keep them between damp paper towels in the fridge.
guide.source: Identification and habitat: The Wildlife Trusts and NC State Extension. Cooking and safety: Colorado State University Extension and NC State Extension.

violets.name: Sweet Violet
violets.description: Small purple flowers with heart-shaped leaves and a sweet fragrance
violets.howTo: Found in woodland edges, hedgerows, and shady areas in early spring

guide.identify: Sweet violet is a low plant with a rosette of long-stalked, heart-shaped leaves with a rounded base, scalloped edges and short hairs; it spreads by long runners that root. Each flower rises on its own stalk from the rosette: five uneven petals, the lowest with a short spur at the back, usually deep violet, sometimes white, with blunt sepals and a sweet scent; dog violets look similar but have no scent. Lesser celandine, which is poisonous and grows in the same places, has glossy, fleshy, hairless leaves and flowers with 8 to 12 shiny yellow petals; lords-and-ladies, also poisonous, has glossy, arrow-shaped leaves with lobes pointing backwards.
guide.habitat: Woodland edges, hedge banks, shady grass, churchyards, parks and old gardens, on moist, rich soil in part shade. It grows across most of Europe and has escaped from gardens in many places; in the US it grows wild locally in lawns and woodland edges.
guide.season: It flowers from February to May, earlier in the mild south, and in April and May in much of the US. A few flowers sometimes appear again in late summer, and the leaves are best young, in spring.
guide.picking: Pick a few flowers and young leaves from each patch and leave the rosette and roots in the ground; never dig up plants. Avoid sprayed lawns, verges and places where dogs are walked.
guide.kitchen: Once identified with certainty, the flowers go raw on salads and desserts, are candied with pasteurised egg white and fine sugar, or are steeped in boiling water and sweetened for violet syrup. Young leaves are eaten raw in salads or cooked like spinach; they are mild and slightly thicken soups. Never eat the roots or seeds, which can cause vomiting, and try a small amount first.
guide.keeps: The flowers wilt fast: keep them between damp paper towels in the fridge and use them the same day. Candied flowers keep in an airtight container in a cool, dark place.
guide.source: Identification and habitat: NatureSpot and NC State Extension. Cooking: Colorado State University Extension and NC State Extension.

amaranth.name: Amaranth
amaranth.description: A leafy green plant, often considered a weed, with edible leaves and seeds rich in nutrients.
amaranth.howTo: Look for it in disturbed soils, gardens, and fields during summer. Young leaves are best harvested before flowering.

guide.identify: Redroot amaranth (pigweed) is a stout, upright annual with a stem covered in fine white hairs, red at the base, and a pink to red taproot. Its alternate leaves are oval to diamond-shaped, smooth-edged and long-stalked, often with a small notch or tiny point at the tip; the tiny green flowers sit in dense, bristly, prickly spikes and later hold tiny, shiny black seeds. Two toxic weeds share its ground: thorn apple (Datura), with large, coarsely toothed, foul-smelling leaves, white trumpet flowers and spiny pods, and black nightshade, with wavy-edged leaves, small white star flowers and black berries.
guide.habitat: Gardens, fields, farmyards and waste ground: bare, rich, disturbed soil in full sun. Native to central and eastern North America, it is a common weed across the US and much of Europe, most of all in warm lowlands.
guide.season: A summer annual: it comes up in late spring once the soil warms, flowers from about July to September and ripens seed from August to October, until the first frost. The leaves are best young, before flowering.
guide.picking: Pick young leaves and tender tops by hand before flowering, and rub out the seed heads once the seeds are black. Avoid roadsides and sprayed fields; skip heavily manured or fertilised ground and drought-stressed plants, which build up the most nitrate.
guide.kitchen: Once identified with certainty, cook the leaves like spinach: boil them briefly and pour the water away, which lowers their nitrate and oxalate. Eat them in moderation, and not at all if you have kidney stones or kidney disease; they taste mild and earthy, good with garlic, beans and eggs. The seeds can be toasted or cooked like a grain.
guide.keeps: The leaves wilt within a day: keep them in a bag in the fridge, or blanch and freeze them. Dry the seed heads in a paper bag, rub out and winnow the seeds and store them in a closed jar.
guide.source: Identification and season: Cornell University and NC State Extension. Nitrates and oxalates: NC State Extension and Michigan State University Extension. Thorn apple mix-ups: Marseille poison control centre.

artichoke.name: Wild Artichoke
artichoke.description: A thistle-like plant with edible flower buds and stems, related to the cultivated artichoke.
artichoke.howTo: Found in meadows and fields, harvest young flower buds and tender stems in spring and early summer.

guide.identify: Wild artichoke (wild cardoon) forms a large rosette of deeply cut leaves, silvery grey-green above and almost white with felted hairs beneath, each lobe ending in a stiff yellow spine. In late spring a stiff, branched stem up to head height carries heads like small artichokes, wrapped in spine-tipped bracts, that open into blue-purple thistle flowers. Atractylis gummifera, a deadly Mediterranean thistle that has been mistaken for wild artichoke and has killed people in Morocco, has no stem: its pink flower head sits flat in the middle of the spiny rosette, it flowers in late summer and autumn, and its root oozes a sticky gum. Never eat a stemless thistle rosette or a thistle root.
guide.habitat: Dry, sunny, open ground: pastures, field edges, roadsides, fallow land and scrub, often on clay. Native to the Mediterranean, from Portugal to Greece and North Africa; in northern and central Europe it is only a garden escape. In California it is an invasive weed of grassland and coastal scrub below 500 m; elsewhere in the US it is a garden plant.
guide.season: The rosette grows after the autumn rains and through the mild winter: leaf stalks are picked from late winter to spring, heads in late spring and early summer. It flowers mainly in June and July, then dries off in the summer drought.
guide.picking: Wear thick gloves and cut stalks or heads with a knife; leave the root, and in its native range leave some heads to flower. In California, where it is invasive, take heads before they seed and never move seed heads; check local rules on public land.
guide.kitchen: Once identified with certainty, peel the leaf stalks of spines and strings, drop the pieces into lemon water, as they blacken, and boil them until tender; they taste like a bitter artichoke and are stewed or fried in batter. From the heads, strip the spiny bracts and eat the tender base and heart. The dried flowers curdle milk for cheeses such as Serra da Estrela and Torta del Casar.
guide.keeps: Stalks keep a few days in the fridge in a damp cloth; boiled, they freeze well.
guide.source: Identification, range and season: IUCN Global Invasive Species Database and California Invasive Plant Council. Atractylis poisonings: Moroccan poison control data.

asparagus.name: Wild Asparagus
asparagus.description: A perennial plant with slender, edible shoots that appear in spring.
asparagus.howTo: Look for young shoots in open fields, meadows, and along hedgerows in spring.

guide.identify: Wild asparagus is a tangled, evergreen, woody shrub up to about 1.5 m with no true leaves, only tufts of short, stiff, needle-like green branchlets, each ending in a sharp spine; its black berries are not eaten. In spring, thin dark green to purplish shoots, often thinner than a pencil, push up from the base of the old spiny bush, with small pointed scales pressed to the stem and no leaves. Black bryony and white bryony, poisonous climbers of the same hedges, also sprout in spring: black bryony soon unfolds glossy heart-shaped leaves, white bryony is hairy with lobed leaves and tendrils. Pick only shoots that rise from an asparagus bush you can see.
guide.habitat: Mediterranean scrub, the edges of holm oak and pine woods, olive groves, hedges, stone walls and roadsides, from the coast into the hills of Portugal, Spain, southern France, Italy, the Balkans and Greece. It does not grow wild in northern and central Europe: asparagus there is garden asparagus gone wild, mostly on sandy ground.
guide.season: Shoots come up from late winter to spring after the autumn and winter rains: from February on warm coasts, into April and May in the hills. Rain followed by mild, sunny days brings a new flush.
guide.picking: Snap each shoot by hand where it breaks easily, leave some on every bush and never cut or uproot the bush. In Italy each region sets its own rules (Tuscany allows picking only until 31 May); in Spain the landowner and the regional government decide, and parks often ban picking: check local rules.
guide.kitchen: Once identified with certainty, use only the tender part above where the shoot snaps; it is more bitter than garden asparagus. Cook it briefly: in omelettes and scrambled eggs, risotto or pasta, or sautéed with garlic and olive oil.
guide.keeps: Best eaten the same day; it keeps a few days in the fridge standing in a little water, or blanch and freeze it.
guide.source: Identification, habitat and season: Mediterranean floras and the University of the Balearic Islands virtual herbarium. Bryonies: RHS. Picking rules: Regione Toscana.

black_chant.name: Black Trumpet (Horn of Plenty)
black_chant.description: A dark, funnel-shaped mushroom with a rich, smoky flavor, prized in gourmet cooking.
black_chant.howTo: Found in deciduous forests, especially under oak and beech, in late summer and autumn.

guide.identify: A thin, hollow horn 4 to 8 cm across, open down to the base, with no separate cap. The inside is grey-brown to black and finely scaly; the outside is ash-grey, smooth or only faintly wrinkled, with no gills or ridges, and turns paler with a whitish bloom as it ripens. The flesh is thin, brittle and grey-black, with a faint, sweet smell. Black trumpets of the eastern US (Craterellus fallax) look the same but give a pinkish-orange spore print rather than white; the ash-grey chanterelle (Craterellus cinereus) has clear forked ridges on the outside.
guide.habitat: It lives with broadleaf trees, mainly beech and oak, also hornbeam and hazel, in damp leaf litter and moss, often in large groups on rich, loamy soil, in gullies and on banks. Common across Europe; in the eastern US its counterpart grows under oak and beech, and on the Pacific coast a western black trumpet grows under tanoak, live oak and madrone.
guide.season: Mainly autumn: in Europe from late summer to November, into December in mild years and later still around the Mediterranean; in the eastern US from July to October after heavy rain. On the Pacific coast the western black trumpet fruits from midwinter into spring.
guide.picking: Pinch or cut at the base, leave the small ones and take only what you will eat; local limits on wild mushrooms apply. It hides well in dark litter: where you find one, look closely around it.
guide.kitchen: Once identified with certainty, split each trumpet lengthwise and rinse out leaves, insects and grit, then drain it well. Never eat it raw: cook it well, in butter, cream sauces, risotto or pasta, or with fish and eggs. The taste is deep and smoky, stronger after drying.
guide.keeps: Fresh, only a few days in the fridge. It dries quickly and very well; keep it in a closed jar, or grind it to a powder for sauces and soups.
guide.source: Identification and habitat: First Nature (UK), MushroomExpert.com and MykoWeb (California Fungi). Season: GBIF records.

lingonb.name: Lingonberry
lingonb.description: Small, red, tart berries that grow on low evergreen shrubs in acidic soils.
lingonb.howTo: Look for them in coniferous forests, moorlands, and heathlands in late summer and autumn.

guide.identify: Lingonberry, also called cowberry, is a creeping evergreen dwarf shrub with thick, glossy, dark green leaves whose edges roll under; the pale underside is speckled with tiny dark dots. Small white to pink bell-shaped flowers in short clusters at the shoot tips give round, glossy red berries that hang in small bunches. Bearberry (Arctostaphylos uva-ursi), a trailing shrub of the same places, has net-veined leaves without dots and dry, mealy berries. The poisonous red and black berries do not grow on a low evergreen carpet: yew (Taxus) is a tree or tall shrub with flat needles and a red cup open at the end around a dark seed; mezereon (Daphne mezereum) is an upright shrub with berries pressed along the stem; deadly nightshade (Atropa bella-donna) is a tall herb with black berries; red baneberry (Actaea) and lily of the valley (Convallaria majalis) are soft herbs.
guide.habitat: Acid, poor soil in pine and spruce forests, birch woods, heaths, moorland and mountain slopes above the treeline; very common in Scandinavia and the Baltic states, and found in the Alps and other mountains. In North America it grows mainly in Canada and Alaska and reaches the US only in the far north, from Minnesota to Maine, where it is rare (endangered in Wisconsin).
guide.season: Berries turn red from August and are best when fully dark red, from September into October; they hang on the plants into winter.
guide.picking: Pick dark red berries by hand, or with a berry picker where that is allowed; in Sweden, Finland and Norway everyman's right lets anyone pick wild berries away from houses and gardens, though nature reserves can have their own rules. In central Europe, Bavaria's health authority (LGL) says eating wild berries has not been shown to be a risk factor for fox tapeworm, but advises washing them well; only heating above 60 °C kills its eggs, and home freezing does not.
guide.kitchen: Raw berries are sour and slightly bitter, so once identified with certainty they are usually cooked with sugar into a sauce or jam, or stirred raw with sugar as in Sweden. Serve them with meatballs, game, roasts, potato pancakes or porridge.
guide.keeps: They keep longer in the fridge than most berries, and stirred with sugar they keep cool for a long time thanks to their natural benzoic acid. They freeze well as they are.
guide.source: Identification and range: Minnesota Wildflowers and CREA Mont-Blanc. Picking rights: Swedish Environmental Protection Agency. Fox tapeworm: Bavarian State Office for Health and Food Safety (LGL).

masterwort.name: Masterwort
masterwort.description: A perennial herb with aromatic leaves and white flower clusters, used in traditional medicine and as a spice.
masterwort.howTo: Found in mountain meadows and forest clearings, harvest leaves and roots in spring and summer.

guide.identify: Masterwort is a hairless umbellifer 30 to 100 cm tall with a round, grooved, hollow stem; its leaves split into three and three again into broad, oval, double-toothed leaflets 5 to 10 cm long, and the upper leaves sit on large, inflated sheaths. The flat white or pinkish umbels have up to 50 rays, the fruits are round, flat and broadly winged, and a crushed leaf or the thick brown rootstock smells strongly spicy, of celery and carrot. Its deadly look-alikes have finely divided, feathery or fern-like leaves: hemlock with a smooth, purple-blotched stem and a mousy smell, fool's parsley with long bracts hanging under each small umbel, cowbane (water hemlock) with a rootstock split into hollow chambers when cut lengthways, hemlock water dropwort with pale tubers in wet ground. Giant hogweed is far bigger, with a bristly, purple-blotched stem and sap that burns skin in sunlight; masterwort's own sap can also make skin sensitive to sunlight.
guide.habitat: Damp mountain meadows, tall-herb stands, stream banks, scree and alder scrub, mostly at 1,400 to 2,700 m, in the Alps, Pyrenees, Carpathians and other mountains of central and southern Europe. In Germany it is native only in the Bavarian Alps; lower down it is rare and usually escaped from old gardens, as in Britain and Scandinavia.
guide.season: The leaves grow as the snow melts and are best young, in early summer. It flowers from late June to August; the fruits ripen in September and October.
guide.picking: Wearing gloves, take a few leaves from a large stand and leave the rootstock in the ground; digging the root often needs a permit (in Tyrol from the district authority), and many reserves and national parks ban picking. It grows among monkshood and white false hellebore, both deadly: pick leaf by leaf from a plant identified whole.
guide.kitchen: Once identified with certainty, use it as a seasoning, not a vegetable: it is strongly bitter and spicy, like lovage. In the Alps the root flavours schnapps (Meisterwurzbrand) and herb cheese; a few young leaves, finely chopped, go sparingly into soups and fresh cheese. Wash your hands after handling it.
guide.keeps: Dry leaves, or slices of root, in an airy, shaded place and store them in a closed jar.
guide.source: Identification, habitat and season: Botanical Society of Britain and Ireland and Alpine floras. Root digging and schnapps: Austrian Ministry of Agriculture (register of traditional foods). Skin reactions: Botanical Dermatology Database.

parasol.name: Parasol Mushroom
parasol.description: A large, tall mushroom with a broad, scaly cap resembling a parasol, edible when young.
parasol.howTo: Look for it in meadows, grasslands, and forest edges from late summer to autumn.

guide.identify: A tall mushroom: the cap opens from a closed, egg-shaped drumstick into a flat umbrella 10 to 25 cm across, cream with brown scales and a smooth brown bump in the centre. The gills are white, free and crowded; the slender stem, up to 30 cm tall with a bulb at the base, has a brown snakeskin pattern and a thick double ring that slides up and down; the spore print is white. The deadly Lepiota species are small, with caps of a few centimetres; Chlorophyllum molybdites gives a greenish spore print; the shaggy parasols (Chlorophyllum rhacodes and C. brunneum), which upset many people, have a smooth stem and flesh that turns orange-red when cut; Amanita pantherina has white warts on the cap, a ring that does not slide and a rimmed bulb at the base.
guide.habitat: In grassland and at woodland edges: pastures, meadows, clearings, rides and dunes, on well-drained soil from the lowlands to the mountains. Common across Europe.
guide.season: Summer to autumn, mainly July to October, and into November in southern Europe. It comes up after a spell of warm, wet weather.
guide.picking: Pick only open, full-size caps whose every feature you can check; lift the whole mushroom to see the base, and leave any parasol-like mushroom with a cap under 10 cm. Leave old, tough ones, and check local rules: many regions limit how much you may pick.
guide.kitchen: Once identified with certainty, eat only the cap, and cook it: like most wild mushrooms it can upset the stomach raw. Breaded and fried like a schnitzel, or grilled with butter and garlic, it tastes mild and nutty. The tough stems can be dried and ground for soups.
guide.keeps: Two days in the fridge. Sliced caps dry well.
guide.source: Identification and habitat: First Nature. Look-alikes and poisonings: ANSES. Season: GBIF records.

sorrel.name: Common Sorrel
sorrel.description: A tangy, lemon-flavored leafy plant often used in salads and soups.
sorrel.howTo: Harvest young leaves in meadows, grasslands, and along paths in spring and summer.

guide.identify: Tender, arrow-shaped leaves whose two pointed basal lobes point backwards, down the stalk; the upper leaves clasp the stem, and a thin, papery sheath wraps the stem where each leaf joins it. From May the flowering stems carry loose spikes of small reddish flowers. Lords-and-ladies (Arum maculatum), which is toxic, has young leaves of a similar shape, but they often carry dark spots, have rounded lobes and grow in woods and hedges rather than open grassland. Never taste a leaf to check it: lords-and-ladies burns the mouth.
guide.habitat: Meadows, pastures, lawns, verges and open woods, from the lowlands into the mountains; very common throughout Europe. In the US it is introduced and scattered, mainly in the north-east, around the Great Lakes, in Oregon and in Alaska, where the smaller sheep's sorrel is far more common.
guide.season: Leaves grow from early spring, in mild places almost all year, and are best young; once the plant flowers, from May, they turn tougher and more bitter, but cut plants send up new ones.
guide.picking: Pick single young leaves from each plant and leave the root; choose meadows that are not sprayed or fertilised, away from roads and dog paths.
guide.kitchen: Once identified with certainty, the leaves are sharply sour, like lemon peel: shred young ones into salads, or cook them briefly into soups, omelettes and sauces for fish and eggs. The sourness is oxalic acid: eat sorrel in moderation and avoid it if you have kidney stones. Cook it in stainless steel or enamel, not aluminium or cast iron.
guide.keeps: Leaves wilt within two or three days in the fridge; cooked down to a purée, sorrel freezes well.
guide.source: Identification and look-alikes: Woodland Trust and Wild Food UK. US range: Flora of North America. Oxalic acid: Wild Food UK. Season: GBIF records.

st_george.name: St. George's Mushroom
st_george.description: A white, firm mushroom with a mealy scent, appearing around St. George's Day in spring.
st_george.howTo: Found in grassy areas, meadows, and along woodland edges in spring.

guide.identify: A stout, fleshy mushroom, white to cream, with a cap 5 to 15 cm across, often lumpy, with an inrolled edge. The gills are white, narrow and very crowded; the thick, solid stem has no ring and no sac at the base; the firm white flesh does not change colour and smells strongly of fresh meal; the spore print is white. The deadly Inosperma erubescens has a pointed, streaky cap, reddens where handled and gives a brown spore print; Entoloma sinuatum can smell mealy too, but its gills turn pink and its spore print is pink. White Amanitas such as the deadly Amanita verna, also out in spring, have a ring and a sac at the base.
guide.habitat: In grass: pastures, mown verges, parks and woodland edges, often by hawthorn, blackthorn and other hedgerow shrubs, mostly on lime-rich ground. It comes back to the same spots for years, often in rings; found across Europe and much sought after in northern Spain and central Italy.
guide.season: Spring, mainly April and May, and into June in the north and in the mountains; it is named after St George's Day, 23 April. A mild, wet spring brings it on.
guide.picking: Cut the stem at the base and leave the small ones; take young, firm caps, as older ones are often full of maggots. Avoid busy verges, and check local rules: some regions require a permit or set a daily limit.
guide.kitchen: Once identified with certainty, eat it cooked: most of the mealy smell goes, and the firm, mild flesh suits omelettes, scrambled eggs, risotto and cream sauces. Cut each one lengthways first to check for maggots.
guide.keeps: Up to two days in the fridge, wrapped in paper. It freezes well after a quick sauté.
guide.source: Identification and habitat: First Nature. Look-alikes: First Nature and ANSES. Season: GBIF records.

truffle_b.name: Black Truffle
truffle_b.description: A highly prized underground fungus with a strong aroma, used in gourmet cuisine.
truffle_b.howTo: Found underground near the roots of oaks and hazelnuts, typically harvested with trained animals in winter.

guide.identify: A round, lumpy tuber, from walnut to fist size, that grows underground. The black skin, reddish when young, is covered in small, hard, many-sided warts. Cut it in half: ripe flesh is purplish-black, marbled with fine white veins that turn reddish-brown in the air, and it smells strong and earthy. Earthballs (Scleroderma), which are poisonous, have a thick, yellowish to brown, scaly skin, a smell of gas and a firm, dark inside; the winter truffle (Tuber brumale) and the imported Chinese truffle (Tuber indicum) look similar but are worth far less.
guide.habitat: Underground among the roots of oaks, above all holm and downy oak, and of hazel, on well-drained, lime-rich soil in sunny hill country; a patch of bare, burnt-looking ground around a tree often shows where it grows. Native to southern France, eastern Spain and central Italy; much of the crop now comes from planted truffle orchards.
guide.season: Winter: it ripens from December to March, and markets peak in January. Storms in late July and August, as it swells, decide the size of the crop.
guide.picking: It is found with a trained dog: dig only where the dog marks, with a small truffle spade, take only ripe truffles and fill the hole again. Truffle hunting is regulated: Italy requires a licence after an exam and its regions set the seasons; Spanish regions set seasons and permits; in France truffles belong to the landowner, and in Germany wild truffles are protected. Check local rules before you look.
guide.kitchen: Once identified with certainty, brush it clean under cold water just before use. Shave or grate it raw over warm dishes, or warm it gently in fat: with eggs, butter, pasta, risotto or potatoes. Long cooking kills the aroma.
guide.keeps: Wrap it in kitchen paper in a closed jar in the fridge, change the paper daily and use it within days, as the aroma fades; eggs kept in the jar take on its scent. Freezing keeps the aroma better than drying.
guide.source: Identification and habitat: CRPF Languedoc-Roussillon and Trufamania. Rules: Italian truffle law 752/1985, Spanish regional rules and German Federal Species Protection Ordinance. Season: GBIF records.

bronze_bolete.name: Bronze Bolete
bronze_bolete.description: A dark bronze to almost black-capped porcino with a pale netted stem and firm white flesh
bronze_bolete.howTo: Look on warm lowland slopes under oak and sweet chestnut, later in the season than the summer bolete

guide.identify: The darkest porcino: the cap is dark chestnut to almost black, often with bronze patches, and stays dry and finely velvety even when wet. The pores are white, then yellow to olive, and do not turn blue. The pale brown stem has a fine brown net, densest at the top, and the very firm white flesh does not change colour when cut. The summer bolete is paler, with a net further down the stem; the devil's bolete (Rubroboletus satanas) and Le Gal's bolete (Rubroboletus legaliae), which share its oak woods, have red pores and bluing flesh.
guide.habitat: Warm, sunny slopes with oak, sweet chestnut and beech, mostly between 200 and 1,000 m. Common around the Mediterranean, in Italy along the Apennines and on the islands; rare in Britain and Germany.
guide.season: From July after summer storms, but mainly in September and October, later than the summer bolete, and into November in the south. It fruits when a soaking rain and cooling soil follow a hot spell.
guide.picking: Cut or twist it out and leave young ones to grow. In Germany it is rare and specially protected: do not pick it there. Italy and Spain have regional permits and daily limits.
guide.kitchen: The firmest of the porcini, with a nutty taste that grows when dried. Once it is identified with certainty, brush it, check for maggots and cook it through, as you would porcini.
guide.keeps: It dries and freezes very well in slices.
guide.source: Identification, habitat and season: Regione Piemonte and First Nature; GBIF records. Protection: BArtSchV (Germany). Cooking: Regione Piemonte.

pine_bolete.name: Pine Bolete
pine_bolete.description: A red-brown capped porcino of pine woods, with a stout reddish netted stem and firm flesh
pine_bolete.howTo: Look in mossy pine and spruce forest on acidic sandy soil, in a late spring flush and again in autumn

guide.identify: The red porcino: the cap is wine-red to mahogany, often bumpy, velvety when young and greasy to slimy when wet, with a whitish bloom at the edge. The short, stout stem is flushed reddish brown with a fine whitish to reddish net, and the white flesh is wine-red just under the cap skin. The pores go from white to yellow and olive and barely change colour when pressed. The bronze bolete is sepia to black with no red; red or orange pores (Rubroboletus satanas) or pink pores with a dark net (Tylopilus felleus) rule it out.
guide.habitat: Mostly with Scots pine and spruce on acid ground, often in moss, and in the mountains also with chestnut, beech and fir, mainly at 400 to 1,400 m. Common in Scandinavia, Scotland's pinewoods and the mountains of central and southern Europe.
guide.season: Often the first porcino of the year and the last: a flush in May and June where it stays cool and moist, and the main crop in September and October, into November and past the first frosts.
guide.picking: Cut or twist it out and do not rake the moss, which shelters the fungus. Many Italian and Spanish regions require a permit, and some Swiss cantons limit amounts: check local rules.
guide.kitchen: Once it is identified with certainty, cook it through like porcini; it is milder and slightly resinous, and very firm young ones need longer cooking. It tints the cooking water green and suits sauces, pickling and drying.
guide.keeps: It dries well in slices; fresh, use it within a day or two.
guide.source: Identification, habitat and season: Regione Piemonte and First Nature; GBIF records. Cooking: Regione Piemonte.

summer_bolete.name: Summer Bolete
summer_bolete.description: The earliest porcino, with a finely cracked pale brown cap and a stem netted from top to bottom
summer_bolete.howTo: Look under oak and beech from late spring, well before the other porcini appear

guide.identify: The summer porcino has a matt, dry, velvety cap, pale hazel to mid-brown, that cracks into a fine network in dry weather; it is never greasy, and its edge is no paler than the centre. Its clearest mark is a raised net that runs down the stem almost to the base. The pores are white, then yellow-olive, and do not change colour; the white flesh is softer than in porcini. The devil's bolete (Rubroboletus satanas) and Le Gal's bolete (Rubroboletus legaliae) share its oak woods but have red pores and bluing flesh; the bitter bolete (Tylopilus felleus) has pink pores and a dark net.
guide.habitat: Oak and sweet chestnut, also beech, lime and birch, at wood edges, in parks and on sunny slopes, from the lowlands to about 1,000 m. Common in central and southern Europe, especially south-west France and Portugal; rare in Britain.
guide.season: The first porcino of the year: from May on low ground and June in the mountains, mainly July to early September after warm rain, until the first autumn cold.
guide.picking: Cut or twist it out and leave small ones. In hot weather many are maggoty: halve them on the spot and leave infested ones in the wood. Many Italian and Spanish regions require a permit.
