guide.kitchen: Many cooks rate it the finest porcino: sweet, nutty and fragrant, for drying, sauces and egg dishes. Once it is identified with certainty, cut away maggoty parts and cook it through.
guide.keeps: It keeps worst of the porcini: cook or dry it the day you pick it.
guide.source: Identification, habitat and season: Regione Piemonte and First Nature; GBIF records. Cooking: Regione Piemonte.

pacific_chant.name: Pacific Chanterelle
pacific_chant.description: A large golden chanterelle of the Pacific Northwest, paler and pinker than its European cousin
pacific_chant.howTo: Look in mossy Douglas fir and hemlock forest once the autumn rains have set in

guide.identify: A large chanterelle, paler and pinker than the European one: the cap is orange-yellow to apricot, and young caps often have fine brownish scales and a pinkish cast, which can vanish in wet weather. The blunt, forking ridges below run down the stem and are pale orange-yellow, usually tinged pink; the stem tapers downward, the flesh is whitish and firm, and the cap bruises yellowish. Jack-o'-lanterns (Omphalotus) and the false chanterelle have thin, crowded true gills; the scaly vase chanterelle (Turbinellus floccosus) is a deep, hollow, orange-red trumpet with coarse scales that upsets many people's stomachs.
guide.habitat: It lives with conifers, mainly Douglas fir and western hemlock, also Sitka spruce, in moss and needle litter in second-growth and old forest, mostly in the lowlands and foothills. It ranges from British Columbia through Washington and Oregon, where it is the state mushroom, to northern California.
guide.season: From September to December, sometimes into January, once the autumn rains have soaked the ground; a dry autumn delays it. Each mushroom grows slowly and can keep growing for weeks in cool, wet weather.
guide.picking: Cut at the base and leave the small buttons to grow on; take only what you will eat. Rules differ by national forest, state and park: some require a free permit and set daily limits, many state parks forbid picking and selling needs a commercial permit, so check with the land manager.
guide.kitchen: Once identified with certainty, brush off needles and soil; rinse only if gritty, then dry, as rain-soaked ones hold water. Never eat it raw: dry-fry it first to drive off the water, then finish in butter. Mild, fruity and firm; good with eggs, cream, pasta, salmon and game.
guide.keeps: Several days in the fridge in a paper bag. Dried, it turns tough: for longer keeping, fry it in butter and freeze it.
guide.source: Identification: MushroomExpert.com and UBC Beaty Biodiversity Museum. Picking rules: US Forest Service. Season: GBIF records.

smooth_chant.name: Smooth Chanterelle
smooth_chant.description: An orange chanterelle whose underside is nearly smooth instead of ridged, with a strong apricot smell
smooth_chant.howTo: Look in southeastern oak woods through the humid summer, often in troops on bare soil

guide.identify: Bright orange-yellow to egg-yolk yellow, 2.5 to 8 cm across, flat at first, later a shallow vase with a wavy edge. Its underside sets it apart: smooth or only shallowly wrinkled, paler than the cap and often pinkish, running down the stem, with no true gills. The stem tapers to the base, the flesh is white and does not change when cut, and the smell is usually strong and sweet, like apricots. Jack-o'-lanterns (Omphalotus illudens), common in the same oak woods, have sharp, crowded true gills, grow in tight clusters from wood or buried roots and are orange inside.
guide.habitat: It lives with oaks and sometimes hickories, in hardwood and oak-pine woods across the eastern US, east of the Rocky Mountains, and is most common in the Southeast. It often comes up in troops on bare or mossy soil along paths, stream banks and road cuts.
guide.season: Summer, from June to September and most often from July, soon after warm, heavy rain in humid weather.
guide.picking: Cut at the base, leave the small ones and take only what you will eat. Rules differ by state, park and national forest, and many state parks forbid picking, so check before you go.
guide.kitchen: Once identified with certainty, brush off the soil; the smooth underside holds little grit. Never eat it raw: cook it well, slowly in butter or in a cream sauce. Fruity and mild like other chanterelles; good with eggs, grits, pasta, chicken and pork.
guide.keeps: A few days in the fridge in a paper bag. Dried, it turns tough: for longer keeping, fry it in butter and freeze it.
guide.source: Identification and habitat: MushroomExpert.com and University of Florida IFAS Extension. Season: GBIF records.

winter_chant.name: Winter Chanterelle
winter_chant.description: A small brown-capped chanterelle on a hollow yellow stem, fruiting on through the first frosts
winter_chant.howTo: Look in mossy conifer litter late in the season, often in dense troops on rotting wood

guide.identify: Small and slim: the cap is 1 to 4 cm, brown to yellow-brown, a thin funnel whose centre opens into the hollow stem. Underneath are blunt, forking ridges, grey to yellowish-grey, running down the stem; the stem is yellow to orange-yellow, hollow and often flattened or grooved. The deadly webcap (Cortinarius rubellus) grows in the same mossy conifer woods: it has a pointed red-brown cap, true rusty-brown gills and a solid stem with faint yellow bands, and it destroys the kidneys. Check every mushroom as you pick and again as you clean: Norway's poison centre advises throwing away the whole basket if you find even one webcap in it.
guide.habitat: On wet, acid ground in conifer woods, mainly under spruce and pine, in moss, at bog edges and on moss-covered rotten logs. Common in northern and central Europe and in the mountains of the south; in North America in the Pacific Northwest, northern California and the northern and eastern conifer forests.
guide.season: Late in the year: in Europe from September until hard frost, often still in November and December; on the US Pacific coast from autumn through winter. It needs a wet autumn, and light frosts do not stop it.
guide.picking: Cut the stems above the moss to keep the basket clean, leave the smallest and keep to local limits, such as small amounts for your own use in Germany. In southern Bavaria and the Bavarian Forest it still carries caesium from Chernobyl, so eat it there only now and then.
guide.kitchen: Once identified with certainty, split the hollow stems and rinse out needles and grit. Never eat it raw: cook it well, in butter, sauces or soups, or with game. Earthy and stronger than its size suggests.
guide.keeps: A few days in the fridge in paper. It dries very well and keeps its flavour for months in a closed jar; it can also be cooked and frozen.
guide.source: Identification: MykoWeb (California Fungi) and First Nature (UK). Deadly webcap: Norwegian Institute of Public Health. Caesium: German Federal Office for Radiation Protection (BfS). Season: GBIF records.

eastern_king.name: Eastern King Bolete
eastern_king.description: The king boletes of eastern oak woods: a tan to lilac-brown cap, white pores that turn yellow with age and a netted stem, never bruising blue
eastern_king.howTo: Look under oak, beech and hickory in eastern hardwood forest from June, a few days after warm summer rain

guide.identify: A small group of eastern king boletes: Boletus variipes has a dry, velvety, tan to grey-brown cap that often cracks; Boletus separans has a lilac-brown to liver-red cap fading to yellow-brown, with lilac on the stem. Both have white young pores turning yellowish, a clear white to brownish stem net and white flesh that does not change colour. Bitter Tylopilus, such as the violet-grey Tylopilus plumbeoviolaceus, have pores that turn pink. Red or orange pores (Neoboletus subvelutipes) or bluing pores and flesh (Boletus sensibilis, Boletus huronensis) mean a toxic bolete.
guide.habitat: With oaks, also beech and other hardwoods, east of the Rockies: most often from New York and the Great Lakes through Pennsylvania and the Appalachians to Georgia and the Ozarks. Boletus nobilis and Boletus atkinsonii belong to the same group.
guide.season: June to September, most of all July and August, after warm, soaking summer rain.
guide.picking: Cut or twist it out and slice it on the spot, as summer kings are often maggoty. Some national forests need a free permit and set daily limits; parks have their own, often stricter rules.
guide.kitchen: Once it is identified with certainty, cook it through like porcini: sauté it, add it to pasta, soups and stews, or dry it for a deeper flavour. Use only firm, fresh ones.
guide.keeps: It dries very well in thin slices; fresh, use it within a day or two.
guide.source: Identification and habitat: MushroomExpert (Michael Kuo). Season: GBIF and iNaturalist records. Rules: US Forest Service.

rocky_king.name: Rocky Mountain King
rocky_king.description: A stout high-mountain porcino with a brick-red to red-brown cap, white pores and a thick pale stem netted at the top
rocky_king.howTo: Look under spruce and fir high in the southern Rockies once the summer monsoon rains arrive, from July to September

guide.identify: A big, stout porcino of the high Rockies with a brick-red to reddish-brown cap, tacky when fresh and often with a whitish bloom when young, redder than the porcini (Boletus edulis) that also grows there. The pores are white and stuffed when young, then yellow and olive, and do not bruise. The thick, pale stem has a fine white net at least near the top, and the white flesh does not turn blue. Aspen boletes (Leccinum) have dark scales on the stem, and orange-capped ones have caused severe stomach poisonings in Colorado; red or orange pores mean a toxic bolete.
guide.habitat: Mainly with Engelmann spruce, also fir and Douglas fir, from about 2,400 m to the tree line, in Colorado, New Mexico and the mountains of Arizona.
guide.season: July to September, sometimes into October: it starts with the monsoon storms and moves upslope through the season; in dry summers it barely fruits.
guide.picking: Twist it out gently, since much of the stem is underground, and leave very maggoty ones. Each national forest sets its own rules, some with a free permit and daily limits.
guide.kitchen: Once it is identified with certainty, remove the yellow, soft pores of mature caps, which can taste bitter and turn slimy, then cook it through like porcini or dry it.
guide.keeps: Dry it in thin slices, or sauté and freeze it.
guide.source: Identification and habitat: Arora and Frank (2014), MushroomExpert and Forage Colorado. Season: GBIF records. Rules: US Forest Service.

lions_mane.name: Lion's Mane
lions_mane.description: A white, shaggy clump of long hanging spines on hardwood trees that cooks up like crab
lions_mane.howTo: Look on wounded or dead oak, beech and maple from late summer into autumn, often high on the trunk. In Europe it is rare and protected in places, so leave it there

guide.identify: A single white, rounded clump 8 to 24 cm across, with no cap or gills: soft spines 1 to 5 cm long hang from it like icicles. It yellows with age; the flesh is white and soft and does not change colour when cut, and the spore print is white. Its relatives coral tooth (Hericium coralloides) and bear's head (Hericium americanum) are branched, with shorter spines.
guide.habitat: From wounds in living broadleaf trees and on dead trunks, most often oak, also beech and maple, often high up. It is found across the US, more in the East; in Europe it is rare, on old beech and oak in ancient woods.
guide.season: Late summer to late autumn, after rain; through winter in warm areas such as California. It often returns to the same tree.
guide.picking: In Europe, leave it: it is rare and protected by law in several countries, including the UK, Poland, Hungary, Croatia, Slovenia and Sweden; photograph it and report the find. In the US, cut fresh white clumps at the base with a knife; national forests and parks may need a permit or ban collecting, so check local rules.
guide.kitchen: Once identified with certainty, cook it: slice it, dry-fry it to drive off the water, then brown it in butter. The mild, sweet taste and stringy texture are often compared to crab; yellowed clumps taste sour.
guide.keeps: A few days in the fridge in a paper bag; freeze it after cooking.
guide.source: Identification and season: MushroomExpert.com and Wild Food UK. Protection: IUCN Red List and the UK Wildlife and Countryside Act 1981.

hen_of_the_woods.name: Hen of the Woods
hen_of_the_woods.description: A big rosette of overlapping grey-brown fronds at the foot of old oaks, with white pores underneath
hen_of_the_woods.howTo: Look at the base of old or dying oaks from late August to October; it often comes back to the same tree year after year. It is protected in parts of central and northern Europe

guide.identify: A rosette 15 to 40 cm across of many overlapping, spoon- to fan-shaped grey-brown caps, each 3 to 14 cm wide, branching from a shared white base. The underside is white with tiny pores, not gills; the flesh is white and firm and does not stain when cut or bruised. The black-staining polypore (Meripilus) has larger, thicker caps that bruise black; the umbrella polypore (Polyporus umbellatus) has round caps on small central stems.
guide.habitat: At the base of old oaks, sometimes on stumps or other broadleaf trees; it rots the roots and comes back to the same tree for years. It is common in the eastern US and rare in the West; in Europe it is uncommon and declining, under old oaks and sweet chestnuts.
guide.season: Late summer to late autumn, mostly September and October, often after the first cool nights that follow rain.
guide.picking: Cut the rosette at the base with a knife, take only fresh, firm ones and leave the tree to fruit again. In Europe it is protected by law in Poland, Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania and red-listed in Germany, Austria and elsewhere: check local rules.
guide.kitchen: Once identified with certainty, cook it thoroughly. Shake and rinse soil and insects from between the caps and trim the tough core; fried or roasted, the caps crisp at the edges and taste rich, earthy and slightly peppery.
guide.keeps: Several days in the fridge in a paper bag. It freezes well after cooking and dries well.
guide.source: Identification and habitat: MushroomExpert.com. Status in Europe: IUCN Red List.

saffron_milk_cap.name: Saffron Milk Cap
saffron_milk_cap.description: An orange cap with darker rings that bleeds carrot-orange milk and bruises green; a favourite in Spain and Italy
saffron_milk_cap.howTo: Look under pines and spruces from late summer to November, into winter on the Mediterranean and US Pacific coasts. Break a gill: the milk must be orange to red, never white

guide.identify: An orange cap with darker concentric rings, rolled under at the edge when young, later funnel-shaped and often blotched green. The crowded orange gills run slightly down the short, hollow orange stem, which often has darker orange pits. Break a gill: the milk is carrot-orange and may slowly turn wine-red, and gills and flesh bruise green. White or yellowing milk means another milk cap, such as the woolly milk cap (Lactarius torminosus), which is pinker, has a woolly, bearded cap edge and grows with birch.
guide.habitat: Under pines, on sandy or lime-rich soil, often in young plantations and grassy clearings; close relatives grow under spruce (Lactarius deterrimus) and fir (Lactarius salmonicolor). Common across Europe and above all in the pine woods of Spain, Portugal and Italy; in North America several related orange-milked species grow under conifers.
guide.season: Autumn: from late summer to November in central and northern Europe. In Mediterranean pine woods it follows the autumn rains, from October into January, and on the US Pacific coast it fruits through the wet winter.
guide.picking: Cut the stem at the base, check it for larvae and leave the small ones. In many regions of Spain and Italy you need a permit or must keep to a daily limit: check local rules.
guide.kitchen: Once identified with certainty, cook it well: grilled with garlic, olive oil and parsley, stewed with potatoes or rice, or with meat. The firm, slightly grainy flesh tastes mild and resinous; slow cooking removes any bitterness. The green stains are harmless, and its pigment can turn urine red, which is harmless too.
guide.keeps: Two days in the fridge. It does not dry well; cook and freeze it, or preserve it in oil or vinegar.
guide.source: Identification and habitat: First Nature. Storage: ANSES. Season: GBIF records.

hedgehog_mushroom.name: Hedgehog Mushroom
hedgehog_mushroom.description: A buff to orange cap with soft spines instead of gills underneath: one of the safest wild mushrooms to learn
hedgehog_mushroom.howTo: Look in mossy conifer and broadleaf woods from late summer to late autumn, often in rings or rows; on the US Pacific coast through the winter. Turn it over: spines, not gills

guide.identify: Turn it over: under the cap are soft, brittle spines 2 to 6 mm long, hanging like small icicles, not gills or ridges; they rub off easily. The cap is 4 to 15 cm, cream to buff or pale orange, dry, velvety and often lumpy; the stem is white, solid and often off-centre, and the firm white flesh bruises slowly yellowish to orange-brown. The smaller, more orange terracotta hedgehog (Hydnum rufescens) and the American Hydnum species have the same soft spines. Other tooth fungi, such as Hydnellum and Sarcodon, are tough, corky or brown and scaly, and many are bitter.
guide.habitat: It lives with conifers and broadleaf trees alike, such as spruce, pine, beech, oak and birch, in moss and leaf litter, often in rings or rows. Common across Europe from the lowlands to the mountains and across North America; on the US Pacific coast several Hydnum species grow under Douglas fir, tanoak and other trees.
guide.season: In central and northern Europe from late summer to late autumn, often until hard frost; later and longer in southern Europe, into winter. On the US Pacific coast it comes with the autumn rains and continues through the winter.
guide.picking: Cut at the base, brush off debris on the spot so it does not lodge in the spines and leave the small ones. In southern Bavaria and the Bavarian Forest it still carries caesium from Chernobyl, so eat it there only now and then.
guide.kitchen: Once identified with certainty, brush the cap; on large ones, rub off the spines, which break off in the pan and can taste bitter. Never eat it raw: cook it well, fried in butter or braised. Mild, nutty and sweet, with a firm, meaty bite; good with eggs, potatoes, game and in sauces.
guide.keeps: Firm as it is, it keeps better than most wild mushrooms: several days in the fridge in paper. For longer keeping, cook it and freeze it.
guide.source: Identification: First Nature (UK) and MykoWeb (California Fungi). Caesium: German Federal Office for Radiation Protection (BfS). Season: GBIF records.

shaggy_mane.name: Shaggy Mane
shaggy_mane.description: A tall white cylinder of shaggy scales on lawns and roadsides that dissolves into black ink within a day of picking
shaggy_mane.howTo: Look on lawns, verges and disturbed ground a few days after autumn rain, and after spring rain too. Pick only young, all-white ones and cook them the same day; avoid busy roads, where it takes up heavy metals

guide.identify: A tall white cylinder, 5 to 15 cm high, covered in shaggy, upturned scales, with a pale brown top; with age it opens into a bell. The crowded gills turn from white to pink to black and dissolve into black ink from the cap edge upwards; the white stem is smooth and hollow, with a thin ring that slides and often drops to the base; the spore print is black. The common ink cap (Coprinopsis atramentaria) has a smooth, grey-brown, finely grooved cap with no shaggy scales and grows in clusters from buried wood. On US lawns, young green-spored parasols (Chlorophyllum molybdites) can look similar, but their gills never turn black.
guide.habitat: Lawns, verges, parks, paths, building sites and other disturbed, grassy ground, often in rows or groups. Common across Europe and North America.
guide.season: Mainly late summer and autumn, a few days after rain, and again in spring; on the US Pacific coast it carries on through the mild, wet winter.
guide.picking: Take only young, closed caps that are white all over, with white gills, and only what you will cook the same day. Avoid busy roads, dumps and polluted ground: it takes up heavy metals.
guide.kitchen: Once identified with certainty, cook it within a few hours and cut away any pink or black part, which turns bitter. Sautéed in butter, or in soups and omelettes, it is mild and delicate. It is not known to react with alcohol, but the common ink cap does, even with drinks taken days before or after the meal: if you are unsure which ink cap you have, do not eat it.
guide.keeps: It does not keep: within a day it turns to ink, even in the fridge. Cook it straight away; cooked, it keeps a day or two in the fridge or can be frozen.
guide.source: Identification and habitat: First Nature and Missouri Department of Conservation. Alcohol reaction: First Nature. Season: GBIF records.

giant_puffball.name: Giant Puffball
giant_puffball.description: A smooth white ball, football-sized or bigger, in meadows and pastures, with firm white flesh like fresh mozzarella
giant_puffball.howTo: Look in meadows, pastures, parks and woodland edges from late summer to autumn, often where nettles grow. Cut every one in half from top to bottom: it must be pure white inside, with no trace of a cap or stem

guide.identify: A smooth white ball, often 20 to 50 cm across, with a thin, leathery skin and no stem, joined to the ground by a cord-like root. Cut every one in half from top to bottom: the inside must be firm and pure white throughout, like fresh mozzarella. Any outline of a cap, gills or stem can mean a young Amanita still in its egg, which can be deadly; a thick, scaly, yellowish skin and a dark, purple-black inside mean an earthball (Scleroderma), which is poisonous. Yellow, olive or brown flesh means the spores are ripening: it is no longer edible.
guide.habitat: Meadows, pastures, parks, gardens, hedgerows and woodland edges on rich ground, often among nettles and often in the same place every year. Widespread in Europe and the eastern US; in the dry interior West the similar western giant puffball (Calvatia booniana) grows in sagebrush and open grassland.
guide.season: Summer to autumn: mainly July to October in Europe, late summer to early autumn in the eastern US. It swells fast after warm, heavy rain.
guide.picking: Cut it at the base and take only firm ones that are white inside; one usually feeds several people. Leave old, yellowing ones to spread their spores, and avoid roadsides and lawns treated with chemicals.
guide.kitchen: Once identified with certainty, peel off the skin, which can be hard to digest, and cook it: thick slices fried in butter, or breaded, taste mild and take up other flavours. Try a small amount the first time.
guide.keeps: Eat it within two days, kept in the fridge, and throw it away once the flesh yellows. Fried slices freeze well.
guide.source: Identification and habitat: Missouri Department of Conservation and First Nature. Storage: ANSES. Season: GBIF records.

matsutake.name: Matsutake
matsutake.description: A firm white-and-brown mushroom with a spicy, cinnamon-like smell, prized above all others in Japan
matsutake.howTo: Look in dry, sandy pine heaths from August in the Nordics, and under conifers and tanoak from September to November in the western US. Never rake the ground. It is red-listed in Sweden and Norway, where logging, not picking, is the threat; US national forests require a permit

guide.identify: A firm, heavy mushroom: the cap is 6 to 20 cm, white with brown fibres and scales (browner in Europe and Asia), its edge rolled in when young. The crowded white to cream gills are attached to the stem; a thick white veil leaves a flaring ring with brown scales sheathing the stem below it, and the solid stem narrows to the base, with no bulb, sac or cup. The smell is strong and spicy, like cinnamon with a note of dirty socks: without it, it is not a matsutake, but smell alone is no proof. Smith's amanita (Amanita smithiana) and the destroying angels (Amanita virosa in Europe, A. bisporigera in the East, A. ocreata in the West) are white too, but have a bulb, sac or warty rings at the very base, a ragged or skirt-like ring and no spicy smell; they destroy the kidneys or liver.
guide.habitat: It lives with trees on poor, well-drained soil. In Europe mainly in Finland, Sweden and Norway, in dry, lichen-rich pine heaths on sand or gravel; in western North America under pines, Douglas fir, hemlock, firs and tanoak, often on sandy or pumice soil; in the East under jack pine, red pine and eastern hemlock, in the north and the Appalachians.
guide.season: In the Nordic countries from August to October, after late-summer rain once nights turn cool; in North America from September to November, into December on the Pacific coast.
guide.picking: Rock it gently out of the ground, then fill the hole and put back the moss and needles; never rake or dig, which damages the fungus and future crops. It is listed as Vulnerable worldwide (IUCN) and red-listed in Sweden and Norway, where the loss of old pine forest, not picking, is the threat; US national forests set their own matsutake permits and limits, so check with the ranger district.
guide.kitchen: Once identified with certainty, wipe it clean and trim the stem base; do not wash it. Never eat it raw; cook it gently and briefly to keep the aroma: sliced and grilled, cooked with rice or in a clear broth. Firm and chewy, with a spicy, pine-like scent.
guide.keeps: Wrapped in paper in the fridge; use it within a few days, before the smell fades.
guide.source: Identification: UBC Beaty Biodiversity Museum and MushroomExpert.com. Look-alikes: North American Mycological Association poisoning reports. Status: IUCN Red List. Picking rules: US Forest Service. Season: GBIF records.

ramps.name: Ramps
ramps.description: America's wild garlic: broad, smooth green leaves on purplish stems that smell strongly of onion and garlic
ramps.howTo: Look in rich, moist hardwood forest in the eastern US from March to May, before the trees leaf out. Take one leaf per plant and leave the bulb; some parks ban picking, and Quebec bans selling them

guide.identify: Two or three broad, smooth, flat leaves rise straight from the ground from a small bulb, each on its own stalk, often purplish-red near the base; they wither by early summer, before a leafless stalk carries a rounded cluster of small white flowers. Crush a leaf: ramps smell strongly of onion and garlic and their deadly look-alikes do not, but the smell stays on your fingers, so after the first few leaves the test proves nothing; check every plant by its leaves and stalks too. False hellebore has pleated leaves set along an upright stem and grows in wet ground; lily of the valley has two or three leaves wrapped around one another at the base; autumn crocus, a garden escape, has stalkless leaves in a tuft; Appalachian bunchflower (Melanthium parviflorum) has similar basal leaves but no onion smell.
guide.habitat: Rich, moist deciduous forest with deep leaf litter, on shaded slopes and in stream bottoms, from Quebec and New England through the Appalachians to Georgia and west to Minnesota.
guide.season: Leaves come up from March in the southern Appalachians and in April and May further north, in the few weeks before the trees leaf out; by late May or June they yellow and die back.
guide.picking: Take one leaf per plant, cut with a knife, and leave the bulb: digging it kills the plant, which needs at least five years from seed to reach picking size. Ramps have declined in parts of their range: Great Smoky Mountains National Park bans picking, some national forests limit it and ban selling, and Quebec lists them as vulnerable and bans their sale; check local rules.
guide.kitchen: Once identified with certainty, the leaves taste of strong garlic and onion: use a few raw, or wilt them briefly into eggs, potatoes, pasta and butter.
guide.keeps: Leaves keep a few days in the fridge in a damp cloth; chopped leaves, ramp butter and pesto freeze well.
guide.source: Identification, habitat and picking: NC State Extension and United Plant Savers. Look-alikes: Vermont Department of Health. Rules: National Park Service, USDA Forest Service and Quebec's environment ministry. Season: GBIF records.

fiddleheads.name: Fiddleheads
fiddleheads.description: The tightly coiled young fronds of the ostrich fern: smooth, bright green, with brown papery scales
fiddleheads.howTo: Look on river floodplains and in moist woods from late April to May, while the fronds are still coiled. Always boil them before eating, and take no more than half the fiddleheads of a clump

guide.identify: Only the ostrich fern is picked. It grows in clumps (crowns) of about three to twelve fiddleheads: tight green coils about 2.5 cm across on a smooth stem with a deep U-shaped groove on its inner side, covered in thin brown papery scales that rub off. Last year's fertile fronds, dark brown, stiff and feather-shaped, often still stand in the clump. Bracken, which is carcinogenic, comes up singly from creeping underground stems, with a fuzzy, round stem, no papery scales and a top that branches in three; other ferns, such as cinnamon fern, have woolly fiddleheads and are not recommended.
guide.habitat: Shaded river floodplains, sandbars and rich, moist woods, often under maple and ash. In the US it is common in the Northeast and around the Great Lakes, south to Pennsylvania and west to the Dakotas, and rare in the West outside Alaska; in Europe it grows along streams in the north and centre.
guide.season: Fiddleheads come up in spring as the ground warms after snowmelt and floods: late April in southern Maine, mid to late May in the far north, into early June in places. Pick them while 5 to 15 cm tall and tightly coiled; within days they unroll and are past eating.
guide.picking: Pick only from healthy clumps with at least four fiddleheads, take no more than half and do not return that season: picking them all weakens or kills the fern. Ask the landowner first; in Germany the wild ostrich fern is protected by law, so leave it there.
guide.kitchen: Never eat fiddleheads raw or lightly cooked: they have caused food poisoning outbreaks (nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea and cramps) investigated by the US CDC. Once identified with certainty, rub off the brown scales, wash them in several changes of cold water, then boil them in small batches in plenty of salted water for 15 minutes, or steam them for 10 to 12 minutes, and throw the water away. Only then sauté them or add them to dishes; they taste of asparagus and green beans.
guide.keeps: Refrigerate and use within a week. To freeze, blanch small batches for 2 minutes, cool in ice water, drain and freeze; they still need the full 15 minutes of boiling before eating.
guide.source: Identification, season, picking and cooking: University of Maine Cooperative Extension. Food poisoning: US CDC. US range: Penn State Extension. Protection in Germany: Federal Species Protection Ordinance (BArtSchV).

cloudberry.name: Cloudberry
cloudberry.description: An amber-orange berry of northern bogs, like a soft raspberry, prized across the Nordic countries
cloudberry.howTo: Look on open bogs and wet heath in Fennoscandia in July and August, when the berries turn from hard red to soft amber-yellow. A frost at flowering time can ruin a year's crop

guide.identify: A low herb, not a shrub, about a hand high, rising from creeping underground stems; each upright shoot carries one to three round, wrinkled leaves with five to seven shallow lobes and a single white flower. Male and female flowers grow on separate plants, so only some shoots bear fruit. The berry looks like a raspberry made of a few large drupelets: hard and red at first, it turns soft and amber-orange when ripe.
guide.habitat: Open bogs, wet heath, mires and tundra, often among sphagnum moss and dwarf birch; common in Norway, Sweden, Finland, the Baltic states and Russia, and found on high moorland in Scotland and northern England. In Germany, Poland and the Czech Republic it survives only in a few bogs as a relic of the Ice Age and is protected or listed as endangered.
guide.season: Flowers in June; berries ripen from mid-July in the south of Scandinavia and the Baltic to August in the far north and in the mountains. A frost at flowering time can ruin a year's crop.
guide.picking: Pick only soft, amber berries that come off easily; hard red ones are not ripe. Everyman's right lets anyone pick them in Sweden, Finland and Norway, but in Nordland, Troms and Finnmark the landowner may ban picking on productive cloudberry bogs, announced by signs or in a newspaper; you may then still eat berries on the spot, and on public land in Finnmark only residents may pick them to sell. Nature reserves can have their own rules, and in central Europe the plant must be left alone: check local rules before you go.
guide.kitchen: Once identified with certainty, eat them fresh with cream or on waffles, or cook them into jam; in Finland the jam goes with warm squeaky cheese (leipäjuusto), and in Sweden over ice cream. The taste is tart and aromatic.
guide.keeps: Ripe berries keep only a day or two in the fridge; they freeze well, and their natural benzoic acid helps the jam keep.
guide.source: Identification and habitat: University of Alberta and Minnesota Wildflowers. Picking rules: Norwegian Environment Agency and Swedish Environmental Protection Agency. Status in central Europe: Czech and German red lists.

huckleberry.name: Huckleberry
huckleberry.description: A purple-black mountain berry of the US Northwest, sweeter and tarter than a blueberry
huckleberry.howTo: Look on subalpine slopes and old burns at 1,000–2,000 m in Montana, Idaho and the Cascades from July to September. Huckleberry patches are bear country: make noise and carry bear spray

guide.identify: A deciduous shrub, usually waist to shoulder high, with slightly angled yellow-green young twigs and thin, oval leaves that end in a point and have finely toothed edges. Creamy-pink, urn-shaped flowers hang singly from the leaf axils in early summer; each gives one purple to reddish-black berry, usually without a pale bloom, with a small crown-shaped ring at the tip. Berries not to eat in the same forests grow differently: twinberry honeysuckle (Lonicera involucrata) has black berries in pairs inside red bracts, and baneberry (Actaea rubra) is a soft herb with clustered red or white berries.
guide.habitat: Mountain conifer forests, open subalpine slopes and old burns, where the shrubs fruit best in sun; from British Columbia south through the Cascades and the Northern Rockies (Washington, Oregon, Idaho, Montana, Wyoming) to California, with outlying stands east to the Black Hills and the upper Great Lakes. In the eastern US the name huckleberry usually means Gaylussacia, a different shrub whose berries hold ten small, hard seeds.
guide.season: Ripens from July at lower elevations to September higher up, with berries ripening a few at a time on each bush. A late frost at flowering can cut the crop.
guide.picking: Pick by hand, berry by berry, without breaking branches. On US national forests, picking for your own use is often allowed, sometimes with a free permit and daily and season limits; commercial picking needs a permit or is closed, and some fields are reserved for tribes, such as part of the Sawtooth Berry Fields in Washington: check the forest's rules. Huckleberry patches are bear country: make noise and carry bear spray.
guide.kitchen: Once identified with certainty, eat them raw or cook them into pies, jam, syrup, pancakes and sauces for game; they are more intense than cultivated blueberries, sweet with a tart edge. Rinse them just before use.
guide.keeps: They keep a few days in the fridge, unwashed and spread out; freeze them on a tray, then bag them.
guide.source: Identification and range: USDA Forest Service (Fire Effects Information System) and University of British Columbia. Picking rules: Gifford Pinchot National Forest. Look-alikes: US National Park Service.

pawpaw.name: Pawpaw
pawpaw.description: North America's largest native fruit: green and mango-shaped, with custardy flesh that tastes of banana and mango
pawpaw.howTo: Look in the understory of river-bottom forests in the eastern US from late August to October, when the fruit softens and drops. Eat only the flesh: the skin and seeds are poisonous

guide.identify: A small understory tree that often forms patches from root suckers, with large, drooping leaves that are widest beyond the middle and smell of green pepper when crushed. Deep maroon, six-petalled flowers appear in spring before the leaves. The fruit is oblong, green to yellow-green, borne singly or in clusters of two to nine, with soft yellow, custard-like flesh around two rows of large, flat brown seeds.
guide.habitat: Moist, rich woods on river floodplains, stream banks and shady lower slopes; native across the eastern US from northern Florida to the Great Lakes and southern Ontario, and west to eastern Nebraska, Kansas, Oklahoma and Texas. It does not grow wild in the western US.
guide.season: Fruit ripens from late August in the south to September and October in the north; a tree's crop ripens over one to two weeks, and ripe fruit drops.
guide.picking: A ripe fruit gives slightly when gently squeezed, like a peach, and smells strongly fruity; skin colour is not a reliable sign. Gather fresh windfalls or shake the trunk gently, check every day or two in season and handle the fruit carefully, as it bruises easily.
guide.kitchen: Once identified with certainty, eat only the flesh: cut the fruit in half lengthwise and scoop the flesh away from the skin and seeds, which must not be eaten or chewed. The flesh tastes of banana and mango and can replace banana in breads, ice cream and puddings; wild fruit can have a bitter aftertaste. Some people react with vomiting or an allergic reaction, so try a small amount first; medical sources also advise against eating it in large amounts over long periods, because the flesh contains annonacin, a compound toxic to nerve cells in laboratory studies.
guide.keeps: Ripe fruit lasts only a few days at room temperature and about a week in the fridge; fruit picked just before it is fully ripe keeps up to three weeks in the fridge and then finishes ripening at room temperature. The scooped flesh freezes for up to a year.
guide.source: Identification and range: University of Kentucky Center for Crop Diversification. Ripeness, preparation and keeping: Purdue Extension. Reactions: Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center.

rose_hips.name: Rose Hips
rose_hips.description: The red autumn fruits of wild roses, rich in vitamin C and full of seeds wrapped in itchy hairs
rose_hips.howTo: Look on hedgerows, scrub and woodland edges from late August to November; they are softest after the first frosts. Remove the seeds and hairs, which irritate the mouth and gut

guide.identify: Dog rose is a shrub with long arching stems, strongly hooked prickles and leaves of 5 to 7 toothed leaflets. The hips are oval, smooth, glossy scarlet and 1 to 2 cm long, with no sepals left on them when ripe; inside, hard seeds sit in fine, irritant hairs. Black bryony, white bryony and bittersweet hang shiny red, poisonous berries in bunches on climbing stems without prickles in the same hedges; a rose hip grows on a prickly rose stem and is full of hairy seeds.
guide.habitat: Hedgerows, scrub, woodland edges and rough grassland across Europe, from the lowlands into the mountains. In the US dog rose grows wild in places, and the hips of native wild roses and of rugosa rose are used the same way.
guide.season: Hips ripen from September to November and many stay on the bush into winter. Frost makes them softer and sweeter, but the longer they hang the less vitamin C they hold.
guide.picking: Pick firm, fully coloured hips that give a little when pressed, a few from each bush, and leave plenty for birds. Wear gloves and avoid roadsides and sprayed hedges.
guide.kitchen: Once identified with certainty, only the pulp is eaten: the seeds and their hairs irritate the mouth, gut and skin. Cut off the stalk and tip, halve the hips and scrape out every seed and hair, or simmer them whole and press them through a fine sieve; then strain the juice again through muslin. Use the pulp for syrup, jelly, jam and tea; it goes well with apple.
guide.keeps: Fresh hips keep about a week in the fridge. They freeze well; seeded halves dried at no more than 50 °C keep for many months in an airtight jar.
guide.source: Identification and habitat: Woodland Trust and The Wildlife Trusts. Season, picking and cooking: University of Alaska Fairbanks Cooperative Extension and Bundeszentrum für Ernährung (BZfE).

sloes.name: Sloes
sloes.description: The small blue-black fruits of the thorny blackthorn, with a dusty bloom and a fiercely sour taste
sloes.howTo: Look on hedgerows and scrubby slopes from September to November; they mellow after the first frosts. Don't crush the stones, and watch for shiny black look-alikes such as buckthorn and deadly nightshade

guide.identify: Sloes grow on blackthorn, a dense, woody shrub with dark bark and side twigs that end in sharp thorns; its white blossom opens in March and April, before the leaves. The fruit is round, about 1 cm across, blue-black with a dusty bloom that rubs off, and grows singly or in pairs along the twigs; inside, green and very astringent flesh surrounds one stone. Buckthorn has shiny black berries in clusters with no bloom; deadly nightshade is a soft, leafy herb, not a thorny shrub, with single shiny black berries each sitting in a green star of sepals.
guide.habitat: Hedgerows, scrub, woodland edges and sunny, stony slopes, often in thickets that spread by suckers. It grows across most of Europe, north and south, from the lowlands into the hills.
guide.season: Sloes ripen from September to November and are ready when they are dark and soft enough to squash between your fingers. They are traditionally picked after the first frost, which splits the skins and softens the fruit so the juice runs out; picking them earlier and freezing them overnight does the same.
guide.picking: Wear gloves: the thorns are long and sharp. Pick from several bushes, leave plenty for birds and avoid roadside hedges and sprayed field edges.
guide.kitchen: Once identified with certainty, sloes are too sour and astringent to eat raw, but they make sloe gin and other liqueurs, such as Spanish pacharán in anise spirit, and a jelly with apples. For gin, prick or freeze them, cover them with sugar and gin, leave them a few months in a dark place, shaking now and then, and strain. Never crush or crack the stones: the kernels contain amygdalin, which releases cyanide.
guide.keeps: Fresh sloes keep a few days in the fridge; frozen in sealed bags they keep for months and go straight from the freezer into the jar.
guide.source: Identification, habitat and the frost tradition: Woodland Trust. Stones: USDA Phytochemical and Ethnobotanical Databases.

sea_buckthorn.name: Sea Buckthorn
sea_buckthorn.description: Bright orange berries packed along thorny, silver-leaved branches: sour and rich in vitamin C
sea_buckthorn.howTo: Look on coastal dunes and gravelly riverbanks from August to October. Wear gloves against the thorns, and check the rules: picking is often forbidden in dune reserves

guide.identify: Sea buckthorn is a thorny, much-branched shrub that forms thickets, with narrow, willow-like leaves covered in silvery scales, above all underneath. Male and female flowers grow on separate bushes, so only female bushes fruit: round, bright orange berries 6 to 8 mm across, packed tightly along the twigs on very short stalks. The berries are juicy and very sour and burst at a touch; rowan and firethorn, by contrast, carry their orange berries in stalked bunches among green leaves.
guide.habitat: It needs full sun and open sand or gravel: coastal dunes of the North Sea, the Baltic and eastern England, and dry gravel banks and terraces of rivers in the Alps and their foothills. In southern Europe it is mostly a plant of mountain river gravels, in the Alps and the Pyrenees; it is also planted on embankments and roadsides.
guide.season: The berries ripen from August into October and are most aromatic early in ripening. They hang on into winter, but overripe berries taste rancid.
guide.picking: Wild stands often grow in dune and riverside nature reserves, where picking is forbidden: check local rules first and never cut branches from wild bushes. Wear gloves, hold a bowl under the twig as you pick because the berries burst, and leave plenty for wintering thrushes.
guide.kitchen: Once identified with certainty, the berries can be eaten raw, but they are very sour, slightly bitter and stain; most are cooked briefly with a little water and honey or sugar, then strained for juice, syrup, jelly or purée. Apple or apricot softens the sharpness; the purée suits yoghurt, muesli, ice cream and soups.
guide.keeps: Fresh berries spoil quickly: freeze them, or freeze the juice in portions. The pulp left after pressing can be dried for tea.
guide.source: Identification and habitat: The Wildlife Trusts and the European Environment Agency (EUNIS). Season, cooking and keeping: Bundeszentrum für Ernährung (BZfE).

boletus.name: Boletus (porcini & bay bolete)
boletus.description: Porcini and the bay bolete in one score: porcini, pine, bronze and summer boletes, the bay bolete in Europe and the North American kings
boletus.howTo: Each place shows the best of their scores; look in beech, oak, chestnut, pine and spruce woods two to four weeks after a soaking rain

guide.identify: The group brings together the porcini (Boletus edulis), the pine, bronze and summer boletes of Europe, the eastern king bolete and Rocky Mountain king of North America, and the bay bolete (Imleria badia). The porcini and kings have white young pores, a stem net and white flesh that does not turn blue; the bay bolete has yellow pores that bruise blue-green and a streaky stem without a net. The cap separates them: brown and greasy (porcini), wine-red (pine), near-black and velvety (bronze), pale and cracked (summer), tan to lilac-brown (eastern king), brick-red (Rocky Mountain king), chestnut and tacky (bay). Red or orange pores mean a toxic bolete such as the devil's bolete (Rubroboletus satanas); pink pores and a dark stem net mean the bitter bolete (Tylopilus felleus).
guide.habitat: All live with trees: porcini with conifers, beech and oak; the pine bolete with pine and spruce; the bronze and summer boletes with oak and chestnut in warm woods; the bay bolete with conifers on acid sand; the eastern king in eastern US oak woods; the Rocky Mountain king under high spruce.
guide.season: Together they run from May, with the summer bolete, to the first frosts, with the bay bolete peaking in October and November; porcini fruit mainly from August to October. Flushes follow a soaking rain by two to three weeks.
guide.picking: Pick only what you can name with certainty and keep each kind apart in the basket. Germany allows porcini only in small amounts for your own use and protects the bronze bolete; Italy and Spain often require permits.
guide.kitchen: Once identified with certainty, all are brushed, sliced to check for maggots and cooked through. The bay bolete gathers radioactive caesium: in parts of Bavaria and Austria eat it only now and then.
guide.keeps: All dry well in thin slices.
guide.source: Identification and habitat: Regione Piemonte, First Nature and MushroomExpert. Season: GBIF records. Rules: BArtSchV (Germany). Caesium: German Federal Office for Radiation Protection (BfS).

cantharellus.name: Chanterelles (all)
cantharellus.description: Every chanterelle in one score: the golden chanterelles, the black trumpet and the winter chanterelle, and in North America the smooth and Pacific chanterelles
cantharellus.howTo: Each place shows the best of their scores; golden chanterelles on mossy slopes under oak, beech and conifers after warm rain, black trumpets in damp leaf litter under broadleaves, winter chanterelles on wet moss under conifers late in the season

guide.identify: Five species: the golden chanterelle, the smooth and Pacific chanterelles of North America, the black trumpet and the winter chanterelle (the last two belong to the close genus Craterellus). All have blunt, forking ridges or a nearly smooth underside running down the stem, never thin blade-like gills. The golden, smooth and Pacific chanterelles are yellow to orange and fleshy with a solid stem; the winter chanterelle is small, with a brown cap and a hollow yellow stem; the black trumpet is a thin, hollow, grey-black horn. Their dangerous look-alikes differ: jack-o'-lanterns (Omphalotus), with true gills and clusters on wood, for the yellow ones, and the deadly webcap (Cortinarius rubellus), with rusty-brown gills, among winter chanterelles.
guide.habitat: All live with tree roots. The golden chanterelle grows under broadleaves and conifers across Europe and North America; the black trumpet in damp leaf litter, mainly under beech and oak; the winter chanterelle on wet moss and rotten wood under conifers. The smooth chanterelle belongs to eastern US oak woods, the Pacific chanterelle to the Douglas fir and hemlock forests of the Pacific Northwest.
guide.season: Together they run from early summer to winter: golden and smooth chanterelles from early summer after warm rain, black trumpets from late summer through autumn, Pacific and winter chanterelles from autumn into winter, until hard frost. In the western US they follow the autumn and winter rains.
guide.picking: Cut or twist at the base, leave the small ones and take only what you will eat. In Germany the golden chanterelle is specially protected and may be picked only in small amounts for your own use; other countries, regions and US public lands set their own limits or permits, so check the local rules.
guide.kitchen: Once each mushroom is identified with certainty, cook them all well and never eat them raw. Golden, smooth and Pacific chanterelles are fruity and firm, best fried slowly in butter; black trumpets are smoky and winter chanterelles earthy, both good in sauces, risotto and with eggs. Split trumpets and winter chanterelles lengthwise to rinse out grit.
guide.keeps: Fresh, a few days in the fridge in paper, not plastic. Black trumpets and winter chanterelles dry very well; golden chanterelles turn tough when dried and are better fried and frozen.
guide.source: Identification and habitat: First Nature (UK), MushroomExpert.com and MykoWeb (California Fungi). Deadly webcap: Norwegian Institute of Public Health. Protection: German Federal Species Protection Ordinance. Season: GBIF records.

bay_bolete.name: Bay Bolete
bay_bolete.description: A chestnut-brown capped bolete, tacky when wet, with cream to olive-yellow pores that bruise blue-green and a streaky stem without a net
bay_bolete.howTo: Look in moss under pine and spruce, also beech and oak, on acid sandy soil from August to the first frosts; it peaks in October as porcini fade. It gathers more Chernobyl caesium than most mushrooms, so in Bavaria and Austria eat it only now and then

guide.identify: A bolete without the porcini's stem net: the cap is chestnut brown, suede-like when dry and sticky when wet. The pores are cream to pale yellow, later olive, and bruise blue-green; the white to pale yellow flesh may turn faintly blue when cut. The slimmer stem is streaked brown on a paler ground. Red or orange pores (Rubroboletus satanas, Neoboletus subvelutipes) or pink pores with a netted stem (Tylopilus felleus) rule it out; in eastern North America, Boletus sensibilis turns dark blue instantly all over and has a yellow stem, and Boletus huronensis is dense and porcini-shaped with a yellowish stem.
guide.habitat: With pine and spruce, also beech, oak and chestnut, on acid, sandy soil, often in moss near old stumps; common in the lowlands of northern and central Europe. In North America in the north-east, the Great Lakes and the Appalachians, under pine and hemlock.
guide.season: In Europe from August to the first hard frosts, peaking in October after the porcini, and into December in the south. In north-eastern North America earlier, mainly July to September.
guide.picking: Twist it out or cut it and leave the young and the old. Check local rules: picking is often banned in nature reserves.
guide.kitchen: Once it is identified with certainty, wipe the cap, peel it if slimy, remove soft old tubes and cook it through; any blue goes in cooking, and the taste is mild. It gathers more radioactive caesium than most mushrooms: in parts of Bavaria and Austria eat it only now and then.
guide.keeps: It dries well in thin slices and freezes after cooking.
guide.source: Identification and habitat: First Nature and MushroomExpert. Season: GBIF records. Caesium: German Federal Office for Radiation Protection (BfS) and Bavarian LGL.
